intro.title: Understanding Matrices
intro.paragraph1: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers used to represent and solve systems of linear equations, transformations, and more compactly than writing out each equation separately. This calculator works with 2x2 matrices — two rows, two columns — the smallest size where every core matrix operation (determinant, inverse, multiplication) is already meaningful. Adding or subtracting two matrices is done entry by entry: each position in the result is just that position's two entries added or subtracted.
intro.paragraph2: Matrix multiplication works differently from ordinary multiplication: each entry of the product A×B is a sum of products — the entry in row i, column j comes from multiplying row i of A against column j of B, term by term, and adding the results. This is also why A×B usually doesn't equal B×A, unlike multiplying ordinary numbers. The determinant, det(A) = a₁₁a₂₂ − a₁₂a₂₁ for a 2x2 matrix, is a single number that captures how the matrix scales area: a determinant of 0 means the matrix squashes every shape down to a line or a point, with no way to undo that — which is exactly why a matrix with determinant 0 (called singular) has no inverse.
intro.paragraph3: When the determinant isn't zero, the inverse A⁻¹ is the unique matrix that undoes A's transformation, satisfying A×A⁻¹ = the identity matrix (1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhere). For a 2x2 matrix, it's found by swapping the two diagonal entries, negating the two off-diagonal entries, and dividing everything by the determinant. The transpose, formed by flipping the matrix across its diagonal (rows become columns), is a much simpler operation that's always defined, regardless of the determinant.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: Representative matrix operations, computed by this calculator.

items.question: Why doesn't A×B equal B×A in matrix multiplication?
items.answer: Because matrix multiplication combines entire rows of one matrix with entire columns of the other, the two orderings genuinely compute different sums — there's no reason for row-times-column in one order to match row-times-column in the other. This makes matrix multiplication non-commutative, unlike multiplying ordinary numbers, and it's one of the first surprising properties students encounter when learning matrix algebra.

items.question: Why does a matrix with a zero determinant have no inverse?
items.answer: The determinant measures how much a matrix scales area (in 2D) or volume (in higher dimensions). A determinant of 0 means the matrix collapses every input onto a lower-dimensional line or point — multiple different inputs get mapped to the same output — so there's no way to reverse that collapse and recover the original input uniquely. A matrix like this is called singular, and the inverse formula would require dividing by that zero determinant, which is undefined.

items.question: What's the difference between the transpose and the inverse?
items.answer: The transpose is purely a rearrangement — it flips the matrix across its diagonal, swapping rows and columns — and it's always defined for any matrix, with no calculation beyond repositioning entries. The inverse, by contrast, is the matrix that reverses A's transformation entirely (A×A⁻¹ = identity), requires dividing by the determinant, and simply doesn't exist when that determinant is zero.

items.question: Can this calculator handle matrices larger than 2x2?
items.answer: Not currently — it's built specifically for 2x2 matrices, which keeps every formula (determinant, inverse, product) a short, exact expression. Larger matrices use the same underlying concepts, but computing a determinant or inverse for a 3x3 or larger matrix requires substantially more involved methods (cofactor expansion, row reduction, or numerical algorithms).

items.question: Why is matrix addition so much simpler than matrix multiplication?
items.answer: Addition combines two matrices the same way you'd add two ordinary grids of numbers — position by position, with no interaction between different rows or columns. Multiplication, by design, is meant to represent composing two transformations (applying one after another), and that composition inherently mixes each row of one matrix with each column of the other, which is why it needs the more involved row-times-column calculation.

items.question: What does it actually mean for a matrix to be singular?
items.answer: A singular matrix — one with a determinant of zero — collapses every point in the plane onto a single line or even a single point, the way matrix [[2,4],[1,2]] squashes the entire plane onto the line y = x/2. Because multiple different starting points end up at the same place, there's no way to reverse that collapse and recover the original input, which is exactly why a singular matrix has no inverse.

items.question: Why does composing two transformations correspond to matrix multiplication?
items.answer: Applying transformation B and then transformation A to a vector v means computing A(Bv). Working through that algebraically — substituting B's effect on each coordinate into A's formula — produces exactly the row-times-column arithmetic that defines matrix multiplication, so (AB)v always equals A(Bv) by construction, not by coincidence.

history.title: A Name Coined Before the Theory Existed
history.paragraph: The word "matrix" entered mathematics in 1850, coined by English mathematician James Joseph Sylvester — but at that point it was just a name for a rectangular array of numbers used to generate determinants, not yet an object with its own algebra. That changed eight years later when Arthur Cayley, a close collaborator of Sylvester's, published "A Memoir on the Theory of Matrices" (1858), the paper generally credited with founding matrix theory as a subject in its own right. Cayley's memoir introduced matrix addition, multiplication, the identity matrix, and the inverse matrix, and proved what's now called the Cayley–Hamilton theorem — all essentially in the single paper that turned Sylvester's naming exercise into a genuine branch of algebra.

modernDevelopments.title: The Twenty-Five-Billion-Dollar Eigenvector
modernDevelopments.paragraph: One of the most consequential modern applications of matrix algebra had nothing to do with physics or engineering: in 1998, Stanford graduate students Larry Page and Sergey Brin built Google's original PageRank algorithm on a matrix eigenvector calculation. Their model represented the entire linked structure of the web as one enormous matrix, where ranking a page's importance came down to finding that matrix's principal eigenvector — the same core operation (matrices acting on vectors) that Cayley formalized in 1858, applied at a scale of billions of web pages instead of the small hand-worked examples of 19th-century algebra.

computationalEra.title: From Punch Cards to Pixels: Matrices in Modern Computing
computationalEra.paragraph: Matrix arithmetic is the literal substrate of modern computer graphics: every GPU is architecturally built to multiply millions of small matrices per second, since every rotation, scaling, and camera projection in a 3D scene is a matrix operation applied to a vertex. The same arithmetic, scaled up to matrices with millions of rows and columns, is also what powers modern neural networks — a network's "forward pass" is, mechanically, a long sequence of matrix multiplications, which is why specialized matrix-multiplication hardware (tensor cores) has become central to modern AI infrastructure.

references.title: Scientific References
references.citation: Higham, N. J. (2008). Cayley, Sylvester, and Early Matrix Theory. Linear Algebra and its Applications, 428(1), 39–43.
references.note: Numerical analyst Nicholas J. Higham's paper, written for the 150th anniversary of Cayley's 1858 memoir, traces the roles Cayley and Sylvester each played in founding matrix theory as a distinct mathematical subject.

variables.title: Understanding Each Operation
variables.intro: Four more matrix relationships worth seeing on their own, each with its own picture instead of just a formula.

determinant.title: Determinant as Area
determinant.description: The determinant isn't just a formula to memorize — it's literally the area of the parallelogram a matrix maps the unit square onto (with a sign: positive when orientation is preserved, negative when the matrix flips the plane over). A matrix that stretches space out has a determinant greater than 1 in absolute value; one that compresses space has a determinant between 0 and 1; and a singular matrix (determinant 0) squashes the entire plane down to a line, which is why it destroys information and can't be undone.
determinant.diagramCaption: Matrix A's image of the unit square, with its area — equal to |det(A)| — shaded and labeled.

composition.title: Matrix Multiplication as Composing Transformations
composition.description: A×B means "first apply B, then apply A to the result" — multiplying two matrices is the same operation as chaining their transformations one after another. That's also the geometric reason A×B usually isn't the same as B×A: transforming a shape with B first and then A doesn't generally land in the same place as doing it in the opposite order, just as rotating a book and then flattening it gives a different result than flattening it and then rotating it.
composition.diagramCaption: The unit square mapped by B alone (orange), and the same square mapped by A×B — B's transformation followed by A's (purple).

inverse.title: The Inverse as an "Undo" Transformation
inverse.description: If A stretches the unit square into a parallelogram, A⁻¹ is the specific transformation that takes that exact parallelogram and folds it back into the unit square — geometrically, applying A and then A⁻¹ (or the reverse) always lands you back where you started, which is what the equation A×A⁻¹ = I actually means. A singular matrix (determinant 0) has no inverse because it has already thrown away information by squashing the plane onto a line, and no transformation can recover a dimension that's already been collapsed.
inverse.diagramCaption: Matrix A's image of the unit square (blue) alongside A⁻¹'s own image of the unit square (teal) — each one undoes the other.

transpose.title: Transpose as a Diagonal Flip
transpose.description: Unlike the other three operations, the transpose isn't really about transforming space at all — it's a purely mechanical rearrangement of the matrix's entries. The two diagonal entries (a₁₁ and a₂₂) stay exactly where they are; the two off-diagonal entries (a₁₂ and a₂₁) simply swap places. That's the entire operation, which is why it's always defined, for any matrix, regardless of the determinant.
transpose.diagramCaption: Matrix A's four entries: the diagonal pair stays fixed, while the off-diagonal pair swaps places to form Aᵀ.

applications.title: Real-World Applications
applications.intro: Matrix operations aren't confined to a linear algebra course — they're the working machinery behind several fields that touch everyday life.

items.title: Computer Graphics: Rotating, Scaling, and Skewing
items.description: Every 2D or 3D graphics engine represents rotation, scaling, and skewing as matrices, and moves an object by multiplying its coordinate vectors by that matrix — exactly the transformation this calculator visualizes for the unit square. Combining several effects (rotate, then scale, then translate) is done by multiplying the individual matrices together first, which is the same composition this page's Matrix Multiplication section illustrates.

items.title: Economics: Input-Output Models
items.description: Wassily Leontief's Nobel Prize-winning input-output model represents an entire economy as a matrix, where each entry captures how much of one industry's output another industry consumes as input. Finding how a change in demand for one product ripples through every other industry comes down to matrix inversion — the same operation this calculator computes for a 2x2 case.

items.title: Cryptography: Hill Ciphers
items.description: The Hill cipher, one of the earliest ciphers to use linear algebra, encrypts a message by multiplying blocks of letters (converted to numbers) by a fixed encryption matrix, and decrypts them by multiplying by that matrix's inverse — which is exactly why the encryption matrix must be invertible (a non-zero determinant) for the cipher to be reversible at all.

items.title: Data Science: Solving Systems of Equations
items.description: Many machine learning and statistics techniques — from linear regression to solving systems of simultaneous equations — reduce to matrix operations under the hood. Finding the best-fit coefficients in a linear regression, for instance, involves multiplying and inverting matrices built from the input data, generalizing the same determinant-and-inverse arithmetic this calculator performs on a 2x2 example.

intro.title: Understanding Molar Mass
intro.paragraph1: Molar mass is the mass of one mole (6.022 × 10²³ particles) of a substance, expressed in grams per mole (g/mol). For a compound, it's found by adding up the atomic mass of every atom in its formula — water, H₂O, has a molar mass of 2×(1.008) + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol, because a water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. This calculator parses the formula you enter, counts every element (including inside parentheses or brackets, like the two hydroxide groups in Ca(OH)₂), and looks up each element's standard atomic weight to compute the total.
intro.paragraph2: The atomic weights this calculator uses are the IUPAC conventional standard atomic weights — essentially a weighted average of an element's naturally occurring isotopes, which is why they aren't whole numbers (chlorine's 35.45 reflects a natural mix of mostly chlorine-35 and some chlorine-37). A handful of the heaviest elements (technetium, promethium, and everything from polonium onward) have no stable isotopes and thus no natural mixture to average — for these, the value in brackets is the mass number of their most stable known isotope instead.
intro.paragraph3: Formulas with a middle dot, bullet, or period followed by a number represent hydrates — compounds that incorporate water molecules into their crystal structure, like CuSO₄·5H₂O (copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate). The number before the water tells you how many water molecules are bound per formula unit of the compound, and this calculator adds that water's mass on top of the anhydrous compound's mass to get the hydrate's total molar mass.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: Molar masses for a range of common compounds, computed by this calculator.

items.question: Why does capitalization matter when typing a formula?
items.answer: Each element symbol is exactly one uppercase letter, optionally followed by one or two lowercase letters — capitalization is how the parser tells elements apart from each other. "Co" is cobalt, but "CO" is two separate elements, carbon and oxygen, forming carbon monoxide; getting the case wrong changes which compound you're actually describing.

items.question: How does this calculator handle groups in parentheses or brackets?
items.answer: It reads everything inside the parentheses or brackets as its own sub-formula, then multiplies every element's count in that sub-formula by the number immediately following the closing bracket (or by 1 if no number follows). In Ca(OH)₂, that means the single oxygen and single hydrogen inside the parentheses each get counted twice, for a total of 2 oxygen and 2 hydrogen atoms.

items.question: What's the difference between molar mass and molecular weight?
items.answer: In practice, essentially nothing for most everyday purposes — both describe the same quantity (the mass of one mole of a substance), and both are typically reported in grams per mole. Chemists mostly use "molar mass" as the more general, formally correct term (it applies equally to ionic compounds and network solids, not just discrete molecules), while "molecular weight" is an older term technically specific to actual molecules.

items.question: Why do some atomic masses have brackets around them?
items.answer: A bracketed value, like technetium's [97], isn't a standard atomic weight at all — it's the mass number of that element's longest-lived known isotope. These elements have no stable isotopes, so there's no naturally occurring mixture of isotopes to average into a standard atomic weight the way there is for something like chlorine or carbon.

items.question: Can this calculator handle formulas with more than one hydrate dot?
items.answer: No — it supports a single hydrate separator (a middle dot, bullet, or period followed by a number), which covers the vast majority of real hydrate formulas like CuSO₄·5H₂O or MgSO₄·7H₂O. Formulas needing more than one such separator are extremely uncommon and outside this calculator's scope.

history.title: A Unit Named for a Word That Wasn't Even About Counting Yet
history.paragraph: The word "mole" entered chemistry in 1893, when German chemist Wilhelm Ostwald defined it in a laboratory manual as simply the mass in grams numerically equal to a substance's molecular weight — at that point a practical shorthand for weighing out chemicals, not yet tied to any specific count of particles. The now-famous number of particles in a mole traces back to Amedeo Avogadro's 1811 hypothesis that equal volumes of gas at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, though Avogadro himself never calculated or named the number that would eventually bear his name.

modernDevelopments.title: From a Named Constant to a Defining One
modernDevelopments.paragraph: French physicist Jean Perrin coined the term "Avogadro's number" in 1908 to honor Avogadro, after Perrin's own experiments on Brownian motion provided the first reasonably precise measurement of that number — work that also helped settle the then-live scientific debate over whether atoms were physically real, and earned Perrin the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics. The relationship between the mole and Avogadro's number was inverted entirely in the 2019 revision of the International System of Units (SI): rather than measuring Avogadro's number from a physical mole defined by carbon-12, the mole is now defined by fixing Avogadro's number at exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³, permanently decoupling the unit from any physical artifact or isotope sample.

intro.title: Understanding Stoichiometry
intro.paragraph1: Stoichiometry is the calculation of how much of each substance participates in a chemical reaction, based on the balanced equation's coefficients. Those coefficients — the numbers in front of each formula, like the 2 in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O — describe a fixed mole ratio: exactly 2 moles of H₂ react with exactly 1 mole of O₂ to produce exactly 2 moles of H₂O, no matter how large or small the actual reaction is. This calculator uses that ratio directly: moles of the target substance equal moles of the known substance multiplied by (target coefficient ÷ known coefficient).
intro.paragraph2: Because chemicals are measured by mass in a lab, not by counting individual molecules, converting to and from moles requires molar mass — the same calculation this site's Molar Mass Calculator performs. Given a known amount in grams, this calculator first divides by the known substance's molar mass to get moles; after applying the mole ratio, if the target amount is wanted in grams, it multiplies the target moles by the target substance's molar mass. Requesting moles on either side skips the corresponding conversion.
intro.paragraph3: This calculator assumes the equation you're working from is already balanced and that the reaction goes to completion with no leftover limiting reagent to account for — it performs the ratio-and-mass arithmetic once the coefficients are known, rather than balancing an unbalanced equation itself (a separate, more involved task that this site's Chemical Equation Balancer handles).

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: Stoichiometric conversions for the reaction 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O (electrolysis/combustion of water) and N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 (ammonia synthesis), computed by this calculator.

rows.calculation: 4 g of H2 (coefficient 2) → grams of H2O (coefficient 2)
2 mol of N2 (coefficient 1) → moles of NH3 (coefficient 2)
32 g of O2 (coefficient 1) → moles of H2 (coefficient 2)

items.question: Why do I need to enter the coefficients myself instead of the full equation?
items.answer: Parsing and correctly balancing an arbitrary chemical equation is a substantially harder problem than applying a ratio once the coefficients are already known — this calculator focuses specifically on the mole-ratio conversion step. If you don't have a balanced equation yet, this site's Chemical Equation Balancer can balance one for you first.

items.question: Does it matter which substance I call "known" and which I call "target"?
items.answer: No — the mole-ratio relationship works symmetrically. Whichever substance you have a measured amount of is the "known," and whichever one you want to find the amount of is the "target"; swapping them and re-entering the numbers the other way around gives you the reverse conversion.

items.question: Why does the calculator need molar mass at all if I'm just using mole ratios?
items.answer: Mole ratios convert moles to moles directly, but in practice you almost always start with (or want) a mass in grams, since that's what a lab balance measures. Molar mass is the conversion factor between grams and moles for each specific substance, so it's only needed at the entry and exit points of the calculation — not in the ratio step itself.

items.question: What happens if I mix up the coefficients from an unbalanced equation?
items.answer: The calculator will still compute a mathematically consistent answer, but it won't reflect real chemistry — the mole ratio has to come from a properly balanced equation to mean anything. Double-check that both sides of your equation have equal numbers of each type of atom before trusting the coefficients you enter.

items.question: Can this handle a reaction with more than two substances at once?
items.answer: Not directly in a single calculation — it converts between exactly one known and one target substance at a time. For a reaction with several products or reactants, run the calculator once per substance you want to find, always using the same known amount and its coefficient as the starting point.

history.title: A Word Coined for the "Art of Measuring" Chemical Elements
history.paragraph: German chemist Jeremias Benjamin Richter coined the term "stoichiometry" in his three-volume 1792–1793 work Anfangsgründe der Stöchyometrie oder Meßkunst chymischer Elemente ("Elements of Stoichiometry, or the Art of Measuring Chemical Elements"). Richter was convinced that chemical reactions followed strict mathematical laws, and his careful measurements of the weights of acids and bases needed to exactly neutralize each other led him to what's now called the law of reciprocal proportions — an early, quantitative precursor to the mole-ratio calculations this calculator performs, worked out decades before atoms or molecules were reliably countable.

modernDevelopments.title: The Reaction That Feeds Roughly Half the World
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ used in this page's worked examples is the Haber-Bosch process, developed by Fritz Haber (lab-scale synthesis, 1909) and industrialized by Carl Bosch (1913) — work that earned each of them a separate Nobel Prize (Haber in 1918, Bosch in 1931). By fixing atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia for synthetic fertilizer at industrial scale, the exact 1:3:2 mole ratio in that single stoichiometric equation is credited with sustaining roughly half of current global food production, since most of the nitrogen in a typical human body today traces back through the food supply to ammonia made this way.

intro.title: Understanding Equation Balancing
intro.paragraph1: Balancing a chemical equation means finding coefficients — whole numbers placed in front of each formula — so that the same number of atoms of every element appears on both sides. This reflects the law of conservation of mass: atoms are rearranged in a chemical reaction, but none are created or destroyed, so whatever elements and quantities go in as reactants must come out, in total, as products.
intro.paragraph2: This calculator uses the "matrix method": it treats each element's atom count across every formula as one linear equation, builds a matrix of all those equations together, and solves for the coefficients using Gaussian elimination with exact fractions (avoiding the rounding errors floating-point arithmetic would introduce). The result is a vector of ratios, which the calculator then scales up to the smallest set of positive whole numbers — the same answer a chemist would eventually reach by trial and error, found systematically instead.
intro.paragraph3: A properly balanced equation should also conserve overall electric charge, not just atom counts, which matters for reactions between ions rather than neutral molecules. This calculator balances neutral-formula equations by atom count alone; for reactions written with explicit ionic charges, a full redox-balancing method (tracking oxidation states and electrons transferred) is needed in addition to what this tool computes.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: Representative equations, balanced by this calculator.

items.question: Why does the balancer ignore coefficients I already typed in?
items.answer: Because a coefficient you guessed might be wrong, and there's no reliable way to tell a deliberately chosen coefficient from an accidental typo. The calculator always solves for coefficients from scratch based on the formulas alone, which guarantees a correct result regardless of what you originally typed.

items.question: Why do the coefficients have to be whole numbers?
items.answer: A chemical equation describes whole molecules or formula units reacting together — you can't have "2.5 molecules" of something take part in a reaction. If the underlying ratio comes out fractional (as it sometimes does partway through the calculation), every coefficient is scaled up by the same factor until all of them land on whole numbers, which keeps the ratios between substances unchanged.

items.question: Why does this tool say an equation "can't be balanced"?
items.answer: Usually because the formulas as written don't actually share the elements needed to balance — for example, if an element appears only among the reactants and never among the products, no set of coefficients can make both sides equal for that element. Double-check every formula for typos or a missing product/reactant before assuming the reaction itself is impossible.

items.question: Can this balance equations involving ions or electric charge?
items.answer: Not on its own — it balances atom counts for neutral formulas, which is exactly what most simple reactions need. Redox reactions written with explicit ion charges (like Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻) also need to conserve total charge and electrons transferred, which requires oxidation-state tracking beyond what this atom-counting method performs.

items.question: Is there always exactly one correct balanced version of an equation?
items.answer: For the reactants and products as given, yes — there's exactly one smallest whole-number ratio, though any multiple of it (4H2 + 2O2 → 4H2O instead of 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O) technically also balances. By convention, and by default in this calculator, the smallest possible whole numbers are reported, since any larger common multiple carries no new information.

history.title: A Law Proven by a Very Careful Set of Scales
history.paragraph: The requirement that a chemical equation must balance traces to Antoine Lavoisier's law of conservation of mass, published in his 1789 Traité élémentaire de chimie. By meticulously weighing every substance involved in a reaction — including gases, which many of his contemporaries didn't bother to capture and weigh — Lavoisier showed that the total mass going into a reaction always equals the total mass coming out. His Traité also popularized writing reactions in the equation-like format that made this conservation principle visually obvious, laying the groundwork for the balanced chemical equations still written the same way today.

modernDevelopments.title: From Trial and Error to a Solvable System
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For most of chemistry's history, equations were balanced by inspection — adjusting coefficients by trial and error until both sides matched, a method that gets unwieldy fast for reactions with many elements or terms. The alternative this calculator uses, sometimes called the algebraic or matrix method, treats each element's atom count as a linear equation and solves the whole system simultaneously; John A. Olson's 1997 Journal of Chemical Education paper analyzed this approach formally, including how to extend it to reactions that also need to balance oxidation and reduction. The same underlying technique — solving for the null space of a matrix — is what modern equation-balancing software, including this tool, actually computes.

class-schedule-builder.title: Class Schedule Builder
class-schedule-builder.description: Build a weekly class schedule and instantly detect time conflicts between classes.

quickReference.title: How Conflict Detection Works
quickReference.intro: Add every class you're considering, with the days and times it meets — the builder checks every pair of classes for overlapping time on a shared day.
quickReference.conflictHint: Two classes only conflict if they share a day AND their time ranges actually overlap. Back-to-back classes (one ending exactly when the other starts) are not a conflict.

result.heading: Schedule Check
result.emptySchedule: Add at least one class to check your schedule.
result.invalidClassTime: Every class needs an end time that's later than its start time.
result.missingDays: Select at least one day for every class.

intro.title: Understanding Schedule Conflicts
intro.paragraph1: A schedule conflict happens when two classes meet on the same day during overlapping time windows, so a student physically can't be in both places at once. Detecting this by eye gets error-prone fast once a schedule has more than a handful of classes, especially when classes meet on different combinations of days — a conflict on Monday might not repeat on Wednesday even for the same pair of classes.
intro.paragraph2: This builder checks every possible pair of classes against each other. For each pair, it first finds which days they share, then — for each shared day — compares their time ranges: if the later start time falls before the earlier end time, the ranges overlap and a conflict is recorded, along with exactly which portion of time overlaps. Classes that end exactly when another begins are deliberately not flagged, since back-to-back scheduling (with zero conflict, only zero passing time) is normal and often unavoidable.
intro.paragraph3: Beyond flagging conflicts, the tool totals the number of instructional hours per week across every class, counted once per day it meets — a schedule with no conflicts can still be flagged as unrealistic later by a student simply by comparing that total against how many hours are actually available in a week.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: Representative scheduling scenarios and what this builder reports for each.

rows.calculation: Two sections of the same course, both Mon/Wed 9:00–10:00

items.question: Why doesn't the tool flag back-to-back classes as a conflict?
items.answer: Because there's no actual time overlap — one class ending at 10:00 and another starting at 10:00 don't compete for the same minute. The builder only flags a conflict when a class's start time falls strictly before another's end time on a shared day, which is the definition of two events genuinely overlapping.

items.question: What counts as a "shared day" between two classes?
items.answer: Any day of the week that both classes have selected. A class that meets Monday/Wednesday/Friday and another that meets only Tuesday/Thursday share no days, so they're compared against each other on zero days and can never conflict, no matter what times they use.

items.question: Does the total weekly hours figure include time between classes?
items.answer: No — it only sums the actual meeting duration of every class, counted once for each day it meets. A class that runs 1 hour on three days a week contributes 3 hours to the total, not the wider span of time between its first and last session.

items.question: Can I check a schedule with classes that span midnight or run overnight?
items.answer: The builder compares start and end times within the same day, so an overnight class needs to be entered as ending by 23:59 on the day it starts; a session that logically continues past midnight isn't represented as a single entry.

items.question: Why does the tool require every class to have at least one day selected?
items.answer: A class with no day assigned can't be checked for conflicts against anything, since conflict detection depends entirely on comparing shared days. Requiring at least one day keeps every class meaningful to the conflict check rather than silently ignored.

history.title: A Problem as Old as the University Timetable
history.paragraph: The class-scheduling (or "timetabling") problem was formalized in computing terms by C.C. Gotlieb, whose 1962 paper "The Construction of Class-Teacher Time-Tables" (Proceedings of the IFIP Congress) described how to represent the constraints of a school timetable — teachers, rooms, and time slots that can't double-book — in a form a computer could search over. Before Gotlieb's formal treatment, timetabling at most institutions was done entirely by hand, often taking staff members weeks to produce a single term's schedule by trial and error.

modernDevelopments.title: Why Conflict-Free Scheduling Is Harder Than It Looks
modernDevelopments.paragraph: In 1976, Shimon Even, Alon Itai, and Adi Shamir proved that even a stripped-down version of the timetabling problem is NP-complete — meaning no algorithm is known that can guarantee an optimal, fully conflict-free schedule for every possible input in a reasonable amount of time as the number of classes grows. That result explains why real institutional scheduling systems rely on heuristics and constraint solvers that search for a good-enough schedule rather than provably the best one. This tool sidesteps that harder problem entirely: rather than trying to construct a conflict-free schedule from scratch, it takes a schedule a student has already built and simply checks it, pairwise, for the overlaps that would make it unworkable.

intro.title: Understanding Citation Styles
intro.paragraph1: A citation style is a standardized way of crediting a source, so that a reader can tell at a glance who wrote something, when, and where it was published — and can track down the original if they want to verify a claim or read further. Every style records the same underlying facts (author, title, year, publisher or journal), but arranges and punctuates them differently, which is why the same source produces three visibly different citations depending on which style a discipline has adopted.
intro.paragraph2: This generator asks for a source's details once and formats them according to all three major styles at the same time. It also follows each style's own rule for how many authors to list by name before switching to "et al.": this tool never truncates the author list in APA until beyond 20 authors, switches to "et al." in MLA once a source has three or more authors, and does the same in Chicago once a source has four or more authors — matching how each style's own official guide handles multi-author sources.
intro.paragraph3: One thing this tool can't do is apply italics: it outputs plain text, since a copy button can't reliably preserve formatting across every word processor and platform. In all three styles, the title of a stand-alone work — a book, or the name of a journal or website — is meant to be italicized, while a title that's part of a larger whole, like a journal article or a web page, takes plain quotation marks instead. Re-apply italics to the container title after pasting a citation into your document.

items.question: Which citation style should I use?
items.answer: It depends on your discipline and, often, your instructor or publisher's specific requirement. APA is most common in the social sciences, MLA in the humanities and literature, and Chicago in history and some social sciences (Chicago also has a separate notes-and-bibliography variant used mainly for footnotes, which this tool doesn't generate — only the author-date reference-list form). When in doubt, check your assignment instructions or a target journal's author guidelines rather than guessing.

items.question: Why do APA and MLA format author names so differently?
items.answer: Each style optimizes for a different kind of scanning. APA reduces first and middle names to initials and uses "&" before the final author, prioritizing compact reference lists in fields with heavily co-authored research. MLA spells out first names in full and uses "and," since literary and humanities scholarship more often cites single or dual-authored works where the full name reads more naturally.

items.question: What does "et al." mean, and when does this tool start using it?
items.answer: "Et al." is Latin for "and others," used to shorten a long author list to just the first author's name. This tool follows each style's own official threshold: APA lists every author by name until a source has more than 20, MLA switches to "et al." at 3 or more authors, and Chicago switches to "et al." at 4 or more authors.

items.question: Why does the citation start with the title instead of an author if I leave the author fields blank?
items.answer: All three styles handle sources with no listed author the same way: since there's no author name to lead with, the title moves into the position an author's name would normally occupy, and everything else in the citation shifts over by one slot. This is standard practice, not a limitation of this tool — it's how a reader is meant to alphabetize an unauthored source in a reference list.

items.question: Does this tool italicize book and journal titles for me?
items.answer: No — the output is plain text. In every style here, the title of a complete, stand-alone work (a book, or a journal's or website's name) is meant to be italicized, while a title that's part of something larger (an article, a web page) takes quotation marks instead, which this tool does apply. After pasting a citation into your document, italicize the container title by hand.

history.title: A Manuscript Style Born in a Single Journal Article
history.paragraph: APA style traces to a seven-page 1929 article in Psychological Bulletin, "Instructions in Regard to Preparation of Manuscript," written by a committee of psychologists, an anthropologist, and journal business managers who wanted a shared standard so that submissions across different psychology journals wouldn't each need reformatting by hand. What started as a short set of house-style rules for one field grew, edition by edition, into the full Publication Manual used across the social sciences today — but the core motivation, making it easier for a reader to locate the source behind a claim, hasn't changed since 1929.

modernDevelopments.title: From Fixed Templates to a Universal Core-Elements System
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For decades, style guides handled new kinds of sources by adding an entirely new template for each format — a template for a book, a different one for a magazine article, another for a film, and so on, which struggled to keep up as online sources multiplied. The 2016 (8th) edition of the MLA Handbook replaced that approach with a single set of nine "core elements" (author, title, container, publisher, date, and so on) that a writer fills in for any source, in any medium, treating the journal, website, or database a source appears in as a "container" that can itself sit inside another container. This tool's own approach mirrors that shift: rather than one rigid template per source type, it fills a small set of shared fields differently depending on whether the source is a book, article, or website.

intro.title: Understanding Area
intro.paragraph1: Area measures how much surface a flat shape covers, expressed in square units — the number of unit squares that would tile the shape exactly. Every plane figure has its own closed-form formula for computing this from a handful of measurable dimensions, derived once and reused forever rather than approximated by actually counting unit squares.
intro.paragraph2: This calculator applies the standard Euclidean-geometry formula for each of eight common shapes, from a square's simple side² to a circular sector's angle-scaled fraction of a full circle's area. Every dimension you enter is validated as a strictly positive number before it's used, since a negative or zero length or angle has no physical shape to correspond to.

variables.title: Variables Involved
variables.intro: Every shape's formula is built from a small vocabulary of measurable dimensions — which ones apply depends on which shape you pick.

items.name: Side Length (s)
items.description: A square's single defining measurement — since all four sides are equal, area is simply that length multiplied by itself.

items.name: Base and Height (b, h)
items.description: Two perpendicular measurements shared by triangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids. Height specifically means the perpendicular distance to the base, which is not necessarily one of the shape's own edges.

items.name: Radius (r)
items.description: The distance from a circle's or sector's center to its edge. Doubling the radius quadruples the area, since area scales with the square of the radius.

items.name: Semi-Major and Semi-Minor Axis (a, b)
items.description: Half of an ellipse's longest and shortest diameters respectively — the two-radius generalization of a circle's single radius.

items.name: Central Angle (θ)
items.description: How wide a sector's pie-slice opens, in degrees out of a full 360° circle — it scales the full circle's area down to the fraction the sector actually covers.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few shapes and the area this calculator returns for each.

applications.title: Area in Practice
applications.intro: Measuring area isn't just a classroom exercise — it's the number several everyday trades and professions actually build their estimates and prices around.

items.title: Land Surveying and Real Estate
items.description: Property deeds, tax assessments, and listing prices are all tied to a parcel's or a home's measured area — surveyors decompose irregular plots into simple shapes like these, sum the pieces, and record the total.

items.title: Construction and Interior Design
items.description: Flooring, tiling, carpet, paint, and drywall are all quoted and purchased by area, so a contractor calculates a room's or a roof's area first to know how much material to order and what the job should cost.

items.title: Agriculture
items.description: Farmers plan seed, fertilizer, and irrigation quantities per unit area of a field, so an accurate field-area figure — often built from several trapezoids and triangles stitched together — directly drives input costs.

items.title: Manufacturing and Materials
items.description: Cutting fabric, sheet metal, or glass to a design efficiently depends on knowing each piece's area, both to price the material and to minimize offcut waste.

items.question: What's the difference between area and perimeter?
items.answer: Area measures the surface a shape covers, in square units; perimeter measures the total length of its boundary, in plain length units. A long, thin rectangle and a square can share the same perimeter while having very different areas, which is why the two need separate formulas rather than one being derivable from the other.

items.question: Why does a triangle only need a base and height, not all three sides?
items.answer: The base-and-height formula (½ × base × height) works for any triangle regardless of its other two side lengths, because "height" here means the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex — a triangle's area depends only on that perpendicular distance, not on how the other two sides are shaped around it.

items.question: Why can't a circular sector's angle exceed 360°?
items.answer: 360° is a full circle, so an angle beyond that would ask for more than the entire circle's area — which isn't a meaningful sector. If you need a full circle's area, use the circle shape directly instead of a 360° sector.

items.question: How is an ellipse's area related to a circle's?
items.answer: A circle is a special case of an ellipse where both axes are equal (semi-major = semi-minor = radius), which is why the ellipse formula (π × a × b) collapses to the familiar π × r² exactly when a and b are both set to r.

history.title: From Land Surveying to Euclid's Elements
history.paragraph: Practical area calculation predates written mathematics itself — ancient Egyptian and Babylonian surveyors needed to re-measure farmland area after the Nile's annual floods redrew field boundaries, and early clay tablets and papyri already show working (if sometimes approximate) rules for rectangles, triangles, and trapezoids. Around 300 BCE, Euclid's Elements organized these practical rules into a rigorous deductive system, proving area formulas from first principles rather than stating them as recipes — the same formulas this calculator still applies today are, for the most part, the ones Euclid formally established over two thousand years ago.

modernDevelopments.title: From Compass and Straightedge to GIS and CAD
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Euclid's proofs handled idealized shapes with straight edges and perfect circles, but real plots of land, building footprints, and manufactured parts are rarely so tidy. Modern surveying and geographic information systems (GIS) extend the same underlying idea — decomposing any closed shape into triangles, or applying the shoelace formula to sum signed area directly from a polygon's vertex coordinates — to measure arbitrarily irregular boundaries from satellite imagery or GPS survey points. Computer-aided design (CAD) software applies the very same closed-form formulas this calculator uses, just computed automatically the moment an engineer sketches a part's geometry rather than by hand.

intro.title: Understanding Surface Area
intro.paragraph1: Surface area is the total area of every face of a 3D solid added together — the amount of material it would take to wrap the solid completely, in square units. Unlike volume, which measures the space a solid encloses, surface area only cares about its outer boundary.
intro.paragraph2: For a cone or square pyramid, this calculator asks for the perpendicular height (the distance straight up from the base to the apex) rather than the slant height along the surface, since the perpendicular height is what's usually easy to measure directly. It then derives the slant height internally using the Pythagorean theorem before applying the surface-area formula.

variables.title: Variables Involved
variables.intro: Every solid's formula reduces to the same small set of measurable edges and radii — which ones apply depends on which solid you pick.

items.description: A cube's single defining edge — since all edges are equal, its six faces are all identical squares of side s.

items.name: Length, Width, Height (l, w, h)

items.name: Radius (r)
items.description: The defining measurement of a sphere, and of the circular base shared by a cylinder and a cone.

items.name: Perpendicular Height (h)
items.description: The straight-up distance from a base to an apex or opposite face — for a cone or pyramid, this calculator converts it into the slant height the surface-area formula actually needs.

items.name: Slant Height
items.description: The distance along a cone's or pyramid's slanted outer surface from the base edge to the apex — derived automatically here via the Pythagorean theorem, rather than asked for directly.

applications.title: Surface Area in Practice
applications.intro: Surface area shows up anywhere a real quantity of material has to cover, coat, or wrap a 3D object.

items.title: Packaging and Manufacturing
items.description: Cardboard, sheet metal, and plastic packaging are cut from flat stock, so a package's surface area directly determines how much raw material — and cost — each unit consumes.

items.title: Painting and Coating
items.description: Paint, primer, and protective coatings are bought and applied by area, so painters and industrial coating operations calculate a surface's total area first to estimate how much product a job requires.

items.title: Heat Transfer and Engineering
items.description: A radiator's or heat sink's surface area governs how quickly it can transfer heat to the surrounding air — engineers deliberately maximize surface area (with fins or ridges) when a design needs to shed heat efficiently.

items.title: Biology
items.description: A cell's or an animal's surface-area-to-volume ratio constrains how efficiently it can exchange nutrients, gases, and heat with its environment — a key reason very small organisms and very large ones have such different body shapes.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few solids and the surface area this calculator returns for each.

items.question: Why does the cone ask for height instead of slant height?
items.answer: A perpendicular height is what most people can measure directly (straight up from the base), while a slant height runs along the cone's slanted surface and is harder to measure by hand. This calculator derives the slant height for you from the radius and perpendicular height using the Pythagorean theorem, so you only need to supply the measurement that's actually easy to take.

items.question: What's the difference between surface area and volume?
items.answer: Surface area totals the area of a solid's outer faces — how much material would wrap it. Volume measures the space enclosed inside it — how much it would hold. Two solids can have the same volume with very different surface areas (a sphere has the least surface area of any shape for a given volume), which is why both measurements matter for different practical questions.

items.question: Why does a rectangular prism need three separate dimensions?
items.answer: A rectangular prism has three pairs of matching rectangular faces (length×width, length×height, width×height), and unlike a cube, none of its three dimensions can be assumed equal to the others — all three are independently needed to compute the total surface area.

history.title: Archimedes and the Sphere Inside a Cylinder
history.paragraph: Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BCE) proved in his treatise On the Sphere and Cylinder that a sphere's surface area equals exactly two-thirds the total surface area of the smallest cylinder that encloses it — a result he considered his finest achievement and reportedly asked to have engraved on his tombstone, alongside a diagram of the sphere and cylinder. That same treatise worked out the surface-area formulas for spheres, cylinders, and cones that this calculator still uses today, more than two thousand years later.

modernDevelopments.title: From Hand-Cut Nets to 3D-Printed Surfaces
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For centuries, working out a complex object's surface area meant physically unfolding it into a flat net or approximating it with the simple solids Archimedes and Euclid had already solved. Modern CAD and 3D-modeling software instead represents any surface — however irregular — as a mesh of many small flat triangles, and sums each triangle's area to compute the total, a technique also used to estimate the surface area of everything from a 3D-scanned manufactured part to a digital terrain model of a mountain range.

intro.title: Understanding Volume
intro.paragraph1: Volume measures how much three-dimensional space a solid encloses, expressed in cubic units — the number of unit cubes that would exactly fill it. Each solid shape has its own closed-form formula derived from its geometry, letting volume be computed directly from a few measurements instead of estimated by physically packing it with unit cubes.
intro.paragraph2: This calculator uses the same dimension fields as the companion Surface Area Calculator for identical shapes — the same radius and perpendicular height describe a cylinder or cone in both tools — so a solid you've already measured for one calculation works immediately for the other.

variables.title: Variables Involved
variables.intro: Every solid's volume formula reduces to the same small set of measurable edges and radii — which ones apply depends on which solid you pick.

items.name: Side Length (s)

items.name: Length, Width, Height (l, w, h)
items.description: The three independent edges of a rectangular prism, multiplied together directly to fill the box they define.

items.name: Radius (r)
items.description: The defining measurement of a sphere, and of the circular base shared by a cylinder and a cone. Volume scales with the cube of the radius for a sphere, and the square of the radius for a cylinder or cone.

items.name: Perpendicular Height (h)
items.description: The straight-up distance from a base to an apex or opposite face — always the perpendicular height, never the slanted distance along a cone's or pyramid's surface.

applications.title: Volume in Practice
applications.intro: Volume answers the practical question of how much space a solid takes up, or how much it can hold or contain.

items.title: Shipping and Storage
items.description: Freight pricing, container loading, and warehouse storage all depend on an item's or a box's volume, so logistics companies calculate it directly to plan how much fits in a given container or truck.

items.title: Construction and Materials
items.description: Concrete, gravel, and fill dirt are ordered by volume, so a contractor calculates the volume of a foundation, footing, or excavation first to know how much material to order.

items.title: Manufacturing and 3D Printing
items.description: A part's volume, combined with a material's density, gives its weight before it's ever produced — useful for costing raw material and for estimating how long a 3D print will take.

items.title: Cooking and Chemistry
items.description: Recipes and chemical formulations scale by volume, and the volume of a container (a mixing bowl, a flask, a tank) sets a hard upper limit on how much liquid or granular material it can safely hold.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few solids and the volume this calculator returns for each.

items.question: Why is a cone's volume exactly one-third of a cylinder's?
items.answer: A cone and a cylinder that share the same base radius and height have a fixed volume ratio of exactly 1:3 — a result provable with calculus (integrating circular cross-sections) but known and used long before calculus existed, since it holds regardless of the specific radius or height chosen.

items.question: Why does a square pyramid's volume include a factor of one-third too?
items.answer: The same 1:3 ratio that relates a cone to its enclosing cylinder also relates a pyramid to its enclosing prism with the same base and height — any pyramid or cone occupies exactly one-third of the prism or cylinder that tightly encloses it, which is why both formulas share that factor.

items.question: Does volume use the same height as surface area for a cone?
items.answer: Yes — both this calculator and the companion Surface Area Calculator ask for the cone's perpendicular height (straight up from the base to the apex), not the slant height. Surface area derives the slant height internally when it needs it; volume never needs slant height at all.

history.title: Archimedes, a Bathtub, and a Crown
history.paragraph: According to a story recorded by the Roman engineer Vitruvius, Archimedes of Syracuse worked out how to measure an irregular object's volume by water displacement while stepping into a bath — reportedly rushing into the street shouting "Eureka" ("I have found it") — after being asked to determine whether King Hiero II's crown was pure gold without damaging it. Archimedes also proved, in his treatise On the Sphere and Cylinder, that a sphere's volume equals exactly two-thirds the volume of the smallest cylinder enclosing it — a companion result to his surface-area finding, and one of the volume formulas this calculator still applies today.

modernDevelopments.title: From Water Displacement to CT Scans
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Archimedes' displacement method still works today for any object you can dunk in water, but modern volume measurement has moved well beyond the bathtub. CT and MRI scanners reconstruct an object's — or an organ's — full 3D shape from cross-sectional images and integrate the enclosed volume numerically, the same cross-section-stacking idea behind a cylinder's πr²h formula, just applied to an irregular shape one thin slice at a time. 3D scanners and CAD software do the equivalent for manufactured parts, computing exact volumes for shapes far too irregular for any closed-form formula.

intro.title: Understanding Step-by-Step Solving
intro.paragraph1: Getting a final answer is only half of what a math problem asks for in most classrooms — showing the reasoning that led there is usually the actual point of the exercise. This solver produces the same intermediate steps a student would write out by hand: isolating a variable, computing a discriminant, finding a common denominator, or applying the power rule term by term.
intro.paragraph2: Four problem types are covered, each with its own well-defined solving procedure: linear equations (isolate x algebraically), quadratic equations (the quadratic formula, handling real, repeated, and complex roots), fraction arithmetic (common denominators and reduction to lowest terms), and polynomial derivatives (the power rule applied term by term).

variables.title: Variables Involved
variables.intro: Each problem type reduces to a small handful of coefficients — the letters below appear throughout the worked steps this solver shows.

items.name: Coefficients (a, b, c, d)
items.description: The fixed numbers multiplying x, or standing alone, in a linear or quadratic equation — everything this solver needs to fully determine the problem.

items.name: Discriminant (D = b² − 4ac)
items.description: A single number computed from a quadratic equation's three coefficients whose sign alone determines whether the equation has two real roots, one repeated root, or two complex roots — before you even finish solving it.

items.name: Numerator and Denominator
items.description: The top and bottom of a fraction — the denominator can never be zero, since division by zero is undefined.

items.name: Coefficient and Power
items.description: Each term of a polynomial is a coefficient multiplying x raised to a power; the power rule differentiates every term independently before the results are added back together.

applications.title: Where These Techniques Show Up
applications.intro: Linear equations, quadratics, fractions, and derivatives aren't just classroom exercises — they're the working vocabulary behind a wide range of practical calculations.

items.title: Physics and Engineering
items.description: Projectile motion, falling objects, and many circuit and structural equations are quadratic in form, so solving for when a projectile lands or a beam reaches a critical stress often comes down to exactly the quadratic formula this solver applies.

items.title: Finance and Business
items.description: Break-even analysis, cost and revenue modeling, and simple interest problems frequently reduce to linear equations — isolating an unknown price, quantity, or rate the same way this solver isolates x.

items.title: Recipes, Mixing, and Ratios
items.description: Scaling a recipe, diluting a solution, or combining two mixtures in a given ratio are fraction-arithmetic problems in disguise — finding a common denominator to combine two quantities correctly.

items.title: Optimization
items.description: Finding a maximum or minimum — the least material for a given volume, the highest profit at a given price — starts with a derivative, since a function's rate of change is exactly zero at its peaks and valleys.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: One problem from each of the four supported types.

items.question: What does it mean when a linear equation has "no unique solution"?
items.answer: It means the x-terms on both sides cancel out completely once you try to isolate x. If what's left is a true statement (like 3 = 3), the original equation holds for every value of x — infinitely many solutions. If what's left is false (like 3 = 7), no value of x can ever make the two sides equal.

items.question: Why does a quadratic equation sometimes have complex solutions?
items.answer: Whenever the discriminant (b² − 4ac) comes out negative, the quadratic formula asks for the square root of a negative number, which isn't a real number — but it is a well-defined complex number (a multiple of i, where i² = −1). This happens whenever the equation's parabola never actually crosses the x-axis.

items.question: Why do fraction results always come back reduced to lowest terms?
items.answer: A fraction like 4/8 and 1/2 represent exactly the same value, so reducing by the greatest common divisor of the numerator and denominator doesn't change the answer — it just expresses it in its simplest, most standard form, which is the conventional way to report a fraction result.

items.question: Why does the derivative of a constant term always come out to 0?
items.answer: A constant term doesn't change as x changes, and a derivative measures the rate of change — so a term with no x in it has a rate of change of exactly zero. In power-rule terms, a constant is x⁰, and the power rule multiplies by that power (0) before reducing it, which always zeroes the term out.

history.title: The Book That Named Algebra
history.paragraph: The word "algebra" comes from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 825 CE by the Persian mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi: Al-Kitāb al-Mukhtaṣar fī Ḥisāb al-Jabr wal-Muqābala ("The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing"). The book systematically classified and solved linear and quadratic equations using verbal, step-by-step procedures — completing a square, balancing terms across an equation — rather than the symbolic notation used today, and it's this systematic, procedural approach to solving equations, more than any single formula, that earns al-Khwarizmi the traditional title "father of algebra."

modernDevelopments.title: From Verbal Procedures to Computer Algebra Systems
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Al-Khwarizmi solved equations entirely in words, since the +, −, and = symbols used today weren't invented until centuries later — French mathematician François Viète introduced systematic symbolic notation in the 1590s, and the modern = sign traces to Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557. That symbolic notation made it possible, in the 20th century, to build computer algebra systems that manipulate equations automatically, and this solver follows the same idea on a small scale: instead of a single opaque answer, it walks through the same named steps — isolating terms, computing a discriminant, finding a common denominator — that al-Khwarizmi's original procedures described in prose.

intro.title: Understanding Percentages
intro.paragraph1: A percentage expresses a number as a fraction of 100 — the word itself comes from the Latin per centum, "by the hundred." Writing a value as a percentage makes it easy to compare quantities of very different sizes on the same scale: whether a class has 20 or 200 students, saying 15% failed a test conveys the same relative information either way.
intro.paragraph2: This tool covers five distinct percentage calculations that are frequently confused with one another: finding a percentage of a number, finding what percentage one number is of another, percentage change (a directional comparison that uses the original value as its base), reverse percentage (working backward from a known result to the original number), and percentage difference (a symmetric comparison that does not treat either value as the "original").

diagram.caption: 27 of these 100 squares are shaded — this is literally what "27%" means: 27 parts for every 100.

intro.paragraph3: The distinction between percentage change and percentage difference trips up even experienced analysts. Going from 80 to 100 is a percentage change of +25%, using 80 (the original value) as the base. But the percentage difference between the same two numbers, which uses their average of 90 as the base instead, is about 22.2% — the same two numbers, two different questions, two different valid answers.

items.question: What's the difference between percentage change and percentage difference?
items.answer: Percentage change is directional and always measures against the original value as its base — going from 80 to 100 is a +25% change, but going from 100 back down to 80 is a −20% change, even though it's the same two numbers. Percentage difference is symmetric: it measures the gap between two values against their average instead, so the percentage difference between 80 and 100 is about 22.2%, not 25%, because it divides by their average (90) rather than by the original value (80).

items.question: Why doesn't increasing a number by 20% and then decreasing it by 20% bring it back to where it started?
items.answer: Because each percentage is calculated from a different base. Increasing 100 by 20% gives 120. Decreasing that new number, 120, by 20% removes 24 (20% of 120), not 20, leaving 96 — not the original 100. The second percentage is always taken from whatever the first calculation produced, not from the original number.

items.question: What's the difference between a percentage point and a percent?
items.answer: If an interest rate rises from 5% to 7%, that is a rise of 2 percentage points — a simple subtraction — but it is also a 40% relative increase in the rate itself (2 is 40% of 5). Both statements are correct; they just answer different questions, and mixing them up is one of the most common errors in financial and political reporting.

items.question: How do I reverse a percentage calculation by hand?
items.answer: Divide the known result by the percentage expressed as a decimal. If 12 is 30% of an unknown number, divide 12 by 0.30 to get 40 — the same calculation this tool's "Reverse" mode performs automatically.

items.question: Why can't the "what percent" or "reverse" modes accept a zero base or zero percentage?
items.answer: Both calculations require dividing by that value, and division by zero is mathematically undefined. Rather than showing a meaningless result, the tool flags these cases directly.

items.question: Where do percentages show up in everyday financial decisions?
items.answer: Interest rates, inflation figures, sales tax, discounts, and investment returns are all expressed as percentages, because doing so lets amounts of very different sizes be compared on the same relative scale rather than as raw, hard-to-compare numbers.

history.title: From "Per Cento" to the Modern % Symbol
history.paragraph: Percentages were used in the commercial arithmetic of medieval Italy's trading cities well before they had a dedicated symbol. Interest, profit shares, and taxes were routinely calculated "per cento" — Italian for "per hundred" — and merchant manuscripts from the 15th century already abbreviate the phrase; a manuscript from around 1425 shows the abbreviation "pc" with a small circle standing in for the Italian ordinal ending, an early ancestor of the modern sign. Over the following two centuries the abbreviation was gradually simplified: by around 1650 it had taken a horizontal fraction-bar form, and by the 19th century the two circles had settled on either side of a diagonal stroke, giving the % symbol still used today.

modernDevelopments.title: Percentages in the Spreadsheet and Data Age
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The arrival of the electronic spreadsheet — starting with VisiCalc in 1979 and followed by Lotus 1-2-3 and Microsoft Excel — turned percentage-based financial modeling from a manual, error-prone exercise into something anyone could recompute instantly by changing a single cell. Percentages remain the default unit for describing change in economics, public health, and data journalism today, precisely because they let readers compare figures of very different scale — a country's GDP growth or a survey's approval rating — on the same intuitive footing.

intro.title: How Tipping Math Works
intro.paragraph1: A tip is calculated as a percentage of the bill, then optionally split evenly across everyone at the table. Because it scales with the bill rather than with the amount of work a server actually did, a percentage tip on an expensive bottle of wine adds far more than the same percentage on a modest plate of food — one reason some diners tip a flat amount on certain high-priced items regardless of the percentage they use for the rest of the check.
intro.paragraph2: Splitting a tip evenly rarely divides into a clean number, which is where rounding comes in. This tool's "round up" option takes each diner's raw share, rounds it up to the next whole currency unit, and folds the small difference into the tip rather than making anyone dig for exact change — a common real-world convenience that changes how the total is distributed, not the tip rate you actually asked for.

items.question: Should I tip on the pre-tax or post-tax bill amount?
items.answer: Most etiquette guides recommend tipping on the pre-tax subtotal, but tipping on the post-tax total is common practice and not considered rude — the difference between the two is usually small.

items.question: What's the difference between a tip and a service charge?
items.answer: A tip is voluntary and discretionary. A service charge — often added automatically for large groups — is typically mandatory and added to the bill by the establishment itself, and it doesn't always go entirely to the staff who served you. Check the receipt to see whether one is already included before adding an additional tip.

items.question: Is tipping mandatory?
items.answer: In most countries, no — it's a voluntary, discretionary sum. In the United States it's such a deeply embedded norm that skipping it for merely below-average (rather than genuinely bad) service is generally considered a breach of etiquette, unlike in many other countries where it isn't expected at all.

items.question: Why do restaurants add an automatic gratuity for large groups?
items.answer: It guarantees fair compensation for serving a large, often multi-course table, and prevents a tip from being silently split too thin across many diners who each assume someone else covered it adequately.

items.question: How does the round-up option change what I actually pay?
items.answer: It doesn't change the tip percentage you asked for — it rounds each diner's share up to the next whole currency unit so nobody needs exact change, with the small difference folded into the tip rather than kept as change.

items.question: How much should I tip for services besides restaurants, like haircuts or delivery?
items.answer: Common general norms in tipping-culture countries: 15–20% for hairdressers and barbers, 10–20% or a flat amount for food delivery depending on distance and conditions, and a few dollars per night for hotel housekeeping — though these vary by country. This tool is built around splitting a restaurant-style bill.

history.title: From European Aristocracy to the American Restaurant
history.paragraph: The word "tip" is not an acronym for "To Insure Promptness" — that's a persistent modern myth. Tipping's actual roots trace to master-servant customs in aristocratic Europe, where a servant could be rewarded with extra money for exceptional service beyond their wages. Wealthy Americans encountered the custom on European travels in the 1850s and 1860s and brought it home to appear sophisticated, but most Americans at the time viewed tipping as condescending and fundamentally undemocratic. It became widespread only after the Civil War, when it spread rapidly through service industries — including railroad companies that hired newly freed Black workers as porters at little or no base wage, expecting tips to make up their income. Several U.S. states, citing exactly this exploitative dynamic, banned tipping outright between roughly 1909 and 1926, though every one of those bans was eventually repealed.

modernDevelopments.title: From Cash on the Table to the Tip Screen
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Card-payment tip prompts and point-of-sale tip screens have extended tipping into venues that never took cash tips before, like coffee counters and self-checkout kiosks — a trend widely discussed under labels like "tip creep" and "tipping fatigue." At the same time, a smaller counter-movement of restaurants has experimented with no-tipping, service-included pricing instead, partly inspired by the model common across Western Europe. Regardless of how a tip is prompted, the underlying arithmetic — a percentage of the bill, split however many ways — is the same calculation this tool automates.

intro.title: How Stacked Discounts Actually Work
intro.paragraph1: A discount is a percentage taken off a price, but when two or more discounts apply to the same item, they don't simply add together. Each successive discount applies to the already-reduced price, not the original one — so a $100 item that gets 30% off first drops to $70, and a further 10% off applies to that $70, not the original $100, bringing it to $63. The combined effect is 37% off, not the 40% you'd get by just adding the two rates.
intro.paragraph2: The same relationship runs in reverse. If you know a sale price and the discount rate printed on the tag, you can recover the original price by dividing the sale price by one minus the discount rate as a decimal — a $70 sale price at 30% off implies an original price of $70 ÷ 0.70 = $100. This is useful for verifying a retailer's claimed "original price," or simply for figuring out what something cost before a markdown you know the rate of.

diagram.caption: Each discount applies to the already-discounted price, not the original — so two discounts stack to less than their sum: 30% + 10% is 37% off in total, not 40%.

items.question: Why isn't 30% off plus 10% off the same as 40% off?
items.answer: Because the second discount applies to the price after the first one, not to the original price. $100 at 30% off is $70; a further 10% off applies to that $70, removing $7, not $10 — for a combined $63 final price, which is 37% off the original, not 40%.

items.question: Does the order of stacked discounts change the final price?
items.answer: No — multiplying percentages together is commutative, so 30% off then 10% off produces exactly the same final price as 10% off then 30% off. A retailer might still restrict the order for business reasons, like excluding an already-clearance item from an additional coupon, but the arithmetic itself doesn't care about order.

items.question: How do I find the original price if I only know the sale price and the discount rate?
items.answer: Divide the sale price by one minus the discount rate expressed as a decimal. A $70 item marked 30% off had an original price of $70 ÷ 0.70 = $100. This tool's "Find Original Price" mode performs exactly this calculation.

items.question: What's the difference between a discount and a markdown?
items.answer: The terms are often used interchangeably, but retailers typically distinguish them: a discount is usually a temporary, promotion- or coupon-driven price cut, while a markdown is usually a longer-term reduction to the standing shelf price meant to clear inventory.

items.question: Why do some stores advertise a discount in dollars and others in percent?
items.answer: Research on discount framing has found that a percentage-off discount tends to look more generous on a lower-priced item, while a dollar-off discount tends to look more generous on a higher-priced item — so retailers often choose whichever framing makes an identical price cut appear larger for that item's price tier.

items.question: Does a bigger percentage discount always mean bigger savings in dollar terms?
items.answer: No. A 50% discount on a $20 item saves $10, while a 10% discount on a $300 item saves $30 — the percentage rate alone doesn't tell you the actual amount saved, which is exactly why this tool always shows both figures side by side.

history.title: How the Fixed Price Tag Made "Percent Off" Possible
history.paragraph: Before the mid-19th century, most retail prices in the United States were individually negotiated through haggling, so there was no single stable reference point for a discount to apply against — a "good deal" was whatever price a particular haggling session produced. That changed with Philadelphia merchant John Wanamaker, who introduced marked, fixed price tags at his Oak Hall clothing store in 1861 and formalized a strict "one price" policy across his stores by 1871, paired with one of the first money-back guarantees in American retail. A fixed, marked price is exactly what makes a later "25% off" sale tag a specific, verifiable claim rather than just another opening bid to haggle down from — the arithmetic this tool automates only means something once there's a stable original price to calculate it against.

modernDevelopments.title: From the Clearance Rack to Black Friday
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The term "Black Friday" didn't start as a retail slogan — Philadelphia police coined it in the 1950s and 60s as a complaint about the traffic jams and unruly crowds that swamped the city the day after Thanksgiving, and local merchants unsuccessfully tried to rebrand it as the friendlier "Big Friday." It wasn't until the term spread nationally in the 1980s that retailers reframed it around the idea of stores finally turning a profit — going "into the black" — for the year. Today's version of the same clearance-sale logic runs largely on software: personalized coupon codes, algorithmically timed flash sales, and abandoned-cart discount emails all apply the identical stacked-percentage math this tool calculates, just triggered automatically instead of printed on a tag.
