intro.title: How Deduplication Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: The naive way to find duplicates — compare every line against every other line — takes time that grows quadratically with the list's size: doubling a list's length roughly quadruples the comparison work, which becomes impractical past a few thousand lines. A hash-based approach sidesteps this entirely by keeping a running set of every line already seen: for each new line, checking whether it's already in that set takes roughly constant time regardless of how large the set has grown, since a hash function converts the line's content directly into a lookup position rather than requiring a scan. This is exactly why deduplication tools, including this one, can process lists with tens of thousands of lines instantly rather than freezing.
intro.paragraph2: This also explains why the settings on this tool matter more than they might first appear. "Case-sensitive" and "trim whitespace" both control what actually goes into the hash function — turning case-sensitivity off means "Apple" and "apple" hash to the same bucket and collapse into one; trimming whitespace means " apple" and "apple" do the same. "Keep first" versus "keep last" doesn't change which lines are considered duplicates at all — only which single copy of each duplicate group is the one that survives into the output, and where it ends up positioned.

diagram.caption: How hash-based deduplication works: each input line is checked against a running set of lines already seen. A new line is added to both the set and the output; a repeat (struck through) is skipped entirely.

items.question: Why does this tool drop blank lines entirely?
items.answer: Blank lines don't carry any meaningful content to deduplicate — a list of five blank lines isn't five different pieces of data, it's just formatting. Dropping them keeps the output focused purely on actual list items, rather than cluttering it with meaningless empty entries.

items.question: What's actually the difference between "case-sensitive" and "trim whitespace"?
items.answer: Case-sensitivity controls letter casing specifically — whether "Apple" and "apple" are treated as the same line. Trimming whitespace is a separate, independent setting that controls leading and trailing spaces — whether " apple" and "apple" are treated as the same line. You can toggle either one independently of the other.

items.question: Why would I ever want to keep the last occurrence instead of the first?
items.answer: Order often carries meaning: in a chronologically appended log or a list where later entries represent updates or corrections to earlier ones, the most recent occurrence of a repeated key is usually the one you actually want to keep, not the oldest. "Keep last" preserves that intent instead of defaulting to whichever came first.

items.question: Does sorting change which lines are considered duplicates?
items.answer: No — sorting only reorders the already-deduplicated output alphabetically; it happens as a separate step after duplicate detection is complete, and has no effect at all on which lines were identified as repeats or which occurrence was kept.

items.question: Is this tool's line-ending handling reliable across Windows, macOS, and Linux files?
items.answer: Yes — the three common line-ending conventions (\r\n on Windows, \n on macOS/Linux, and the older \r alone) are all recognized and normalized automatically, so pasting a list exported from any of these systems works correctly without manual cleanup.

items.question: Why does the duplicates list show a count next to each repeated line?
items.answer: The count is the total number of times that exact line appeared in your original input, including the one copy that was kept — so a count of 3 means two copies were removed, not three. This makes it possible to spot which values were duplicated most heavily at a glance, not just that duplicates existed somewhere.

history.title: From Punch-Card Sorting to the Hash Table
history.paragraph: Before hash tables existed, finding duplicates in a large dataset meant sorting it first — an approach with roots in mechanical punch-card sorting machines used for census and business data processing in the early-to-mid 20th century, where physically ordering cards made matching records against each other practical at scale. The conceptual breakthrough that made lookup-based deduplication possible arrived with Hans Peter Luhn's internal IBM research in the 1950s on hashing, formally published by his colleague W. W. Peterson in 1957 — introducing the idea of computing a numeric address directly from a piece of data's content, rather than needing to search or sort for it.

modernDevelopments.title: From Punch Cards to Instant Browser-Based Deduplication
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Hashing became a foundational tool across computing well beyond deduplication — it underpins database indexing, caching systems, and cryptographic fingerprinting alike. What's changed most for a tool like this one specifically is where the computation happens: modern JavaScript engines run hash-based Set and Map operations fast enough to deduplicate substantial lists instantly inside a web browser, on data that never leaves the user's device — a capability that would have required a dedicated server-side batch process not many years ago.

intro.title: How Invoice Totals Actually Add Up
intro.paragraph1: An invoice's math follows a fixed order that matters: every line item's quantity times its unit price is summed into a subtotal, a discount (if any) is subtracted from that subtotal first, and only then is tax calculated — on the discounted amount, not the original subtotal. Applying tax before the discount, or applying it to the pre-discount subtotal, produces a different, incorrect total, which is exactly the kind of ordering mistake this tool's calculation logic is built to never make.
intro.paragraph2: The distinction between an invoice's issue date and its due date is also more than a formality: the gap between them (this tool defaults to 14 days, but 30 is common under the term "Net 30") is the actual interest-free credit period a seller is extending to a buyer, which is why standard payment terms like "Net 30" or "Net 60" are really shorthand for a specific amount of short-term financing built into the transaction.

diagram.caption: The fixed order of invoice math: discount is subtracted from the subtotal first, and tax is calculated on what's left — never on the original subtotal.

items.question: Is a discount applied before or after tax?
items.answer: Before — a discount reduces the subtotal first, and tax is then calculated on that already-discounted amount. Applying tax to the original subtotal and then subtracting the discount produces a different (and incorrect) total whenever both a discount and a tax rate are in play, which is why the order genuinely matters.

items.question: What's the difference between an invoice and a receipt?
items.answer: An invoice is a request for payment, issued before money changes hands, and it establishes a debt the buyer owes. A receipt is proof that payment has already been received. The same document can't correctly serve as both at once — a paid invoice is typically followed by a separate receipt, not relabeled as one.

items.question: What does "Net 30" actually mean?
items.answer: It means full payment is due within 30 days of the invoice's issue date — not 30 days after the goods or services were delivered, and not 30 calendar days from an arbitrary date. "Net 15" and "Net 60" follow the same logic with a different day count; the "Net" simply signals no early-payment discount applies to the stated amount.

items.question: Why does every invoice need a unique invoice number?
items.answer: It's the specific reference both the buyer's and seller's accounting systems use to match a payment to the exact invoice it settles, and in most tax jurisdictions, sequential invoice numbering is also a compliance requirement that makes it harder to conceal deleted or backdated invoices during an audit.

items.question: Is this tool's invoice legally compliant for my country?
items.answer: This tool covers the fields most jurisdictions commonly require, but exact legal requirements vary by country — some require a tax registration number, a specific VAT breakdown, or a particular language. Treat this as a strong starting template, not a substitute for checking your local tax authority's specific invoicing rules.

items.question: Why show the currency explicitly instead of assuming everyone uses the same one?
items.answer: Because an invoice with an ambiguous currency is a real, common source of payment disputes in cross-border business — "$500" alone doesn't specify US, Canadian, Australian, or several other dollars, and stating the currency code (USD, EUR, AED) removes that ambiguity entirely.

history.title: 5,000 Years Before the First Spreadsheet
history.paragraph: The invoice is one of the oldest surviving forms of business documentation: archaeologists have recovered clay tablets from the Sumerian city of Uruk, dating to roughly 3400–3300 BCE, recording deliveries of grain, wool, and beer to temple estates — administrative proof that a transaction had actually taken place. These tablets predate even the earliest fully developed writing systems, meaning record-keeping needs are part of what drove writing itself to be invented, not the other way around. The core function hasn't changed in five millennia: a durable, portable record establishing what was owed, by whom, for what.

modernDevelopments.title: From Paper Ledgers to Structured Data
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For most of that history, an invoice was whatever the seller wrote down — free-form, unstructured, and readable only by a human. That changed with electronic invoicing standards like UBL (Universal Business Language), standardized internationally as ISO/IEC 19845, which defines a strict, machine-readable XML structure for an invoice's fields — issuer, buyer, line items, tax breakdown — so accounting software on both ends of a transaction can process it automatically without a human re-typing anything. Government-mandated e-invoicing built on standards like this is now routine across the EU, and in Turkey, Peru, Colombia, and Panama, among others.

intro.title: How Inventory Costing Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: When a business buys the same product at different prices over time — a common reality as suppliers raise prices or run promotions — it has to decide, on paper, which purchase price to assign to the units it sold and which price to assign to the units still sitting on the shelf. This is not a physical question about which literal box left the warehouse; it is an accounting convention. FIFO assumes the oldest purchase layer is sold first, leaving the newest, usually more expensive, cost basis in ending inventory. LIFO assumes the opposite: the newest layer is sold first, leaving the oldest, usually cheaper, cost basis behind. Weighted-average sidesteps the ordering question entirely by blending every purchase into one cost per unit and applying it uniformly.
intro.paragraph2: The choice is not cosmetic — it changes reported numbers. In a period of rising prices, FIFO assigns the cheaper, older cost to Cost of Goods Sold, which inflates reported profit and the tax bill that follows it, while leaving a higher-value ending inventory on the balance sheet. LIFO does the reverse: it assigns the pricier, newer cost to COGS, shrinking reported profit and tax exposure, while leaving a lower, often stale-looking inventory value on the balance sheet. Weighted-average lands in between, smoothing out the swings of individual purchase lots. None of the three methods is 'more correct' in isolation — they simply answer 'what did this sale cost us?' with three different, equally defensible conventions.

diagram.caption: The same three purchase layers, drawn down in opposite order: FIFO consumes the oldest (bottom) layer first; LIFO consumes the newest (top) layer first.

items.question: Which costing method should my business actually use?
items.answer: It depends on your reporting goals and, in many jurisdictions, on tax rules — under IFRS, LIFO is not permitted at all, while US GAAP permits it. FIFO tends to mirror the physical flow of perishable or fast-moving goods and produces a balance sheet inventory value closer to current replacement cost. LIFO can reduce taxable income during inflationary periods. Weighted-average is often chosen for its simplicity when individual purchase lots are hard to track separately, such as with bulk commodities.

items.question: Why do FIFO, LIFO, and weighted-average give different ending inventory values from the exact same purchases?
items.answer: Because each method makes a different assumption about which purchase price gets assigned to the units that were sold versus the units left in stock. The total units and the total dollars spent purchasing them are identical across all three methods — only how that total is split between Cost of Goods Sold and ending inventory value changes.

items.question: Does the costing method have to match the actual physical order units leave the warehouse?
items.answer: No. FIFO and LIFO are accounting cost-flow assumptions, not requirements about physical handling. A warehouse can physically ship its oldest stock first (a real FIFO picking policy) while its books are kept on LIFO, or vice versa — the accounting convention and the physical logistics are independent decisions.

items.question: Why does weighted-average recompute a single unit cost instead of tracking layers?
items.answer: Because it treats every unit in stock as interchangeable rather than tied to a specific purchase lot. The average cost is simply total cost of all purchases divided by total units purchased — every unit sold or remaining is valued at that same blended rate, which is why weighted-average is the simplest method to compute by hand.

items.question: How does this tool decide which units are 'sold' when I enter a units-sold number?
items.answer: It draws down your purchase batches in the order you entered them (oldest first) for FIFO, in reverse order for LIFO, and applies the single blended average cost for weighted-average — this calculator does not change your batch order for you, so enter batches from oldest purchase to newest for the layer logic to be correct.

items.question: What does the low-stock flag mean, and does it change with the costing method?
items.answer: It compares your ending unit count — the number of units left after the units-sold figure is subtracted — against the reorder threshold you set. The unit count itself is identical across FIFO, LIFO, and weighted-average, since costing method only changes the dollar value assigned to those units, not how many there are.

history.title: A Debate as Old as Modern Accounting
history.paragraph: First-in-first-out and last-in-first-out costing both emerged as formal accounting practices in the United States in the early 20th century, but LIFO's use accelerated sharply after the US Congress formally permitted it for tax purposes in the Revenue Act of 1938 — a period of rising raw material costs where LIFO's lower reported profit meant a lower tax bill. The choice between FIFO and LIFO became one of the most studied topics in accounting research through the mid-20th century, since it directly affects reported earnings, tax liability, and how comparable one company's financial statements are to another's.

modernDevelopments.title: One Global Standard Diverges from the Other
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The clearest modern development is a split rather than a convergence: International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), under IAS 2, prohibit LIFO entirely, while United States Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (US GAAP) continue to permit it. This means a multinational company can be required to report different inventory values for the same physical stock depending on which accounting standard applies, and it is a standing obstacle to full convergence between the two global accounting frameworks. Weighted-average costing, permitted under both standards, has correspondingly grown in popularity as a method that avoids this jurisdictional divide.

intro.title: How Break-Even Analysis Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: Every unit sold contributes a fixed amount — its contribution margin, price minus variable cost — toward covering the business's fixed costs, which don't change no matter how many units are sold. The break-even point is simply the moment those accumulated contributions exactly equal the fixed costs: sell fewer units than that and the business runs at a loss, sell more and every additional unit's contribution margin becomes pure profit, since the fixed costs are already fully covered.
intro.paragraph2: This is exactly why a business with high fixed costs but a high contribution margin per unit (like software, where marginal cost per additional user is near zero) can be unprofitable at low volume and extremely profitable at scale, while a business with low fixed costs but thin per-unit margins breaks even quickly but scales up profit much more slowly. The same math extends past simply breaking even: adding a target profit on top of fixed costs and dividing by the contribution margin answers a more useful real question — not "when do I stop losing money," but "how many units get me to the profit I actually want."

diagram.caption: The classic CVP chart: fixed costs set a flat floor, total cost rises with volume, revenue rises faster — the crossing point is the break-even point, splitting the chart into a loss zone and a profit zone.

items.question: What's the difference between a fixed cost and a variable cost?
items.answer: A fixed cost stays the same regardless of sales volume — rent is rent whether you sell 10 units or 10,000. A variable cost scales directly with each unit sold — the materials in one more product, the commission on one more sale. Break-even analysis treats these two categories completely differently precisely because they behave differently as volume changes.

items.question: Why does the contribution margin matter more than the profit margin here?
items.answer: Because contribution margin (price minus variable cost) tells you exactly how much each additional sale contributes toward covering fixed costs — and once fixed costs are fully covered, every further unit's contribution margin becomes pure profit. Overall profit margin blends fixed and variable costs together, which hides that specific mechanic.

items.question: Can a business ever break even in dollars but not in units, or vice versa?
items.answer: No — break-even units and break-even revenue are two views of the exact same point, since break-even revenue is just break-even units multiplied by the price per unit. They always describe the identical moment where total revenue equals total cost.

items.question: Why round break-even units up instead of to the nearest whole number?
items.answer: Because a fractional unit isn't a real sale — 333.3 units doesn't cover fixed costs, only 334 whole units does. Rounding down would show a break-even point the business hasn't actually reached yet, which defeats the purpose of the calculation.

items.question: Does break-even analysis account for changing prices or costs over time?
items.answer: No — this is a snapshot model that assumes fixed costs, variable cost per unit, and price all stay constant across the full range being analyzed. It's most accurate for a specific planning period at a specific price point, and needs to be recalculated whenever any of those three inputs actually change.

items.question: What does it mean if a break-even calculation returns no valid answer?
items.answer: It means the price per unit doesn't exceed the variable cost per unit — every sale loses money before fixed costs even enter the picture, so no volume of sales, however large, could ever reach break-even. That's a pricing problem, not a volume problem, and no amount of extra sales fixes it.

history.title: From a 1903 Chart to a Depression-Era Standard
history.paragraph: The graphical idea behind break-even analysis dates back further than the term itself: engineer Henry Hess published an early chart plotting cost against volume in 1903, and Charles E. Knoeppel formalized the distinction between fixed and variable costs in 1918. It was Columbia University professor Walter Rautenstrauch who, in his 1930 book The Successful Control of Profits, coined the actual term "break-even point" and popularized the chart as a standard planning tool — timing that mattered enormously, since the Great Depression's collapse in demand forced businesses across the board to understand exactly how far sales could fall before they started losing money.

modernDevelopments.title: From a Hand-Drawn Chart to a Spreadsheet Input
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Break-even analysis is now a standard component of management accounting and startup financial planning, taught as part of cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis in virtually every accounting curriculum. Its modern extensions include multi-product break-even analysis (blending several products' different contribution margins into one combined break-even point) and sensitivity analysis, which tests how the break-even point shifts if a specific cost or price assumption turns out to be wrong — exactly the kind of instant recalculation this tool's live chart is built to show.

intro.title: Understanding Function Graphing
intro.paragraph1: A graph turns an abstract rule — for every x, compute this y — into a shape you can see: a line, a curve, a wave. That shape often reveals things a table of numbers hides at a glance, like where a function crosses zero, where it's increasing or decreasing, or where it has a peak, a dip, or a gap.
intro.paragraph2: This tool works by sampling: it evaluates your expression at 300 evenly spaced x-values across the range you choose, then connects the resulting points with straight line segments. Any x-value where the expression is undefined — such as 1/x at x = 0, or sqrt(x) for a negative x — is simply skipped, which is why a graph can show a visible break or gap instead of a continuous line.

variables.title: Variables Involved
variables.intro: A handful of concepts describe any graph, regardless of which function produced it.

items.name: Independent Variable (x)
items.description: The input you choose freely — this tool samples it at 300 evenly spaced values across your chosen minimum and maximum.

items.name: Dependent Variable (y)
items.description: The output computed from x by your expression — plotted on the vertical axis, one value for each x sampled.

items.name: Domain
items.description: The set of x-values for which the expression is actually defined — a gap in the graph marks an x-value outside the domain, like x = 0 for 1/x.

items.name: Intercepts
items.description: The specific points where a graph crosses the x-axis (y = 0) or the y-axis (x = 0) — often the first landmarks worth reading off a graph.

applications.title: Graphing in Practice

items.question: Why does my graph look jagged or blocky instead of smooth?
items.answer: The tool plots 300 sample points across your chosen range and connects them with straight segments. Over a very wide range, those 300 points get spread thin, so a fast-changing function (like a high-frequency wave) can look more angular than it really is — narrowing the x-range gives the same 300 points more detail to work with.

items.question: Why do some graphs have a visible gap or break in them?
items.answer: That happens at any x-value where the expression is mathematically undefined — dividing by zero (1/x at x = 0), taking the square root of a negative number (sqrt(x) for x < 0), or a similar case. Rather than guessing, the tool simply omits that point, which shows up as a break in the line.

items.question: What functions and operators are supported?
items.answer: Arithmetic operators + − * / ^ (power), the trigonometric functions sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, sqrt, abs, natural log ln, base-10 log log, exp (e^x), max, and min, plus the constants pi and e. Parentheses can be nested freely to control order of operations.

items.question: Why does changing the minimum and maximum x change the shape I see?
items.answer: The range doesn't change the function itself, only which slice of it you're looking at — the same way zooming a map doesn't change the terrain, only how much of it fits on screen. A function like x^3 can look almost flat near the origin and dramatically steep once the range widens, because it's the same curve at a different scale.

history.title: The First Calculator You Could See a Curve On
history.paragraph: Casio released the fx-7000G in October 1985 — the world's first hand-held graphing calculator sold to the public. It packed 82 scientific functions into a device that could also plot them as a line graph or a bar chart directly on its small LCD screen, letting a student see a parabola or a sine wave instead of just computing isolated points on it. Texas Instruments followed a few years later with the TI-81 in 1990, which became a fixture of American algebra and precalculus classrooms for the next decade. The core idea both machines introduced — sampling a function at many points and drawing the result as a curve — is exactly what this browser-based tool still does, just without the dedicated hardware.

modernDevelopments.title: From Dedicated Hardware to the Browser
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Standalone graphing calculators are still standard equipment in many classrooms, but the same sampling-and-plotting technique now runs natively in a web browser, in tools like this one, and in full computer algebra systems (Desmos, GeoGebra, Wolfram Alpha) that can also solve, differentiate, and manipulate the underlying expression symbolically rather than only plotting it. The core visual literacy the fx-7000G first put in students' hands — reading a curve's shape to understand a function's behavior — remains exactly the same skill these newer tools are built around.

intro.title: Understanding Line-by-Line Calculators
intro.paragraph1: A notepad calculator sits between a plain text editor and a spreadsheet: you write the way you'd jot notes on paper — a mix of labels, context, and numbers — and any line that looks like a calculation gets solved automatically next to it, without switching to a separate calculator app or building out spreadsheet cells and formulas.
intro.paragraph2: This tool evaluates every line from top to bottom. A line written as "name = expression" both computes a result and stores it under that name, so any later line can reference it — letting a running total, a tax rate, or a unit price be defined once near the top and reused throughout the rest of the note. Lines that are pure prose, headings, or blank simply produce no result, which is expected rather than an error, since the whole point is mixing notes and math freely in the same document.

items.name: Note

applications.intro: Mixing plain notes with live arithmetic fits naturally into everyday tasks that a plain calculator app or a full spreadsheet would over- or under-serve.

items.title: Budgeting and Bill-Splitting
items.description: Listing rent, utilities, and shared costs as labeled lines — then dividing a running total among roommates — keeps both the math and the reasoning behind it visible in one place.

items.title: Shopping and Unit Pricing

items.description: Sketching out a rough estimate — a tip, a discount, a unit conversion — alongside the context that produced it is faster than opening a spreadsheet for a single calculation.

items.title: Meeting Notes and Planning
items.description: A budget proposal, a project timeline, or a trip-planning note can carry its own supporting math inline, so the numbers stay attached to the notes that explain them instead of living in a separate file.

items.question: Why do some lines show no result at all?
items.answer: Only lines the tool can parse as a calculation or a variable assignment get a result. A line of plain prose, a heading, or a blank line simply isn't one of those — it's treated as a note, not an error, since a notepad calculator is meant to hold both freely.

items.question: How do variables carry from one line to the next?
items.answer: A line matching "name = expression" is evaluated and stored under that name in order, from the top of the note down. Any line below it can then use that name in its own expression — so defining rent = 1200 once lets every later line reference rent without retyping the number.

items.question: Can I reuse a variable name for something else further down?
items.answer: Yes — a later "name = expression" line overwrites the earlier value for every line that follows it. Lines above the reassignment still reflect whatever value was in effect when they were evaluated, since the tool works strictly top to bottom.

items.question: Why does a result sometimes show more or fewer decimal places than I expected?
items.answer: Results are rounded to 8 decimal places and trailing zeros are dropped, so 10 / 4 shows as 2.5 rather than 2.50000000 — this keeps whole numbers and simple fractions readable without hiding meaningful precision on numbers that need it.

history.title: The App That Put an Answer Column Next to Your Notes
history.paragraph: Acqualia Software released the first version of Soulver in 2005, introducing what's now considered the modern notepad calculator interface: a plain-text editor with a live "answer column" running down the right-hand side, showing the result of any line that looked like a calculation. A follow-up update the next year, Soulver 1.2, went further by letting a line mix ordinary words with numbers — "rent 1200 + utilities 85" — and still evaluate correctly, rather than requiring a line to be pure arithmetic. That combination — free-form text, inline results, and variables that carry down the page — is the same model this browser-based tool follows.

modernDevelopments.title: From a Single App to a Whole Category
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Soulver's answer-column idea has since spread well beyond one app: Numi, SpeQ, and several browser extensions offer the same free-text-plus-live-math interface, and general-purpose note apps like Obsidian and Notion have added plugins that evaluate inline math the same way. The underlying technique — parsing free text line by line, evaluating what looks like an expression, and carrying named values forward — is now a small, well-established category of tool rather than one app's novelty.

intro.title: Understanding GCF and LCM
intro.paragraph1: The greatest common factor (GCF) of a set of numbers is the largest whole number that divides all of them evenly — the biggest piece they can all be evenly split into. The least common multiple (LCM) is the smallest whole number that all of them divide into evenly — the first point where their multiples line up. They answer opposite questions: GCF looks for the largest shared divisor, LCM looks for the smallest shared multiple.
intro.paragraph2: This calculator finds both by prime factorization: breaking each number down into the primes that multiply together to make it, then comparing those factorizations. The GCF takes every prime factor the numbers share, at the lowest power any of them uses it; the LCM takes every prime factor that appears in any of them, at the highest power it's used. For exactly two numbers, GCF × LCM always equals the product of the two numbers — a useful check on the result.

variables.title: Variables Involved
variables.intro: Every GCF/LCM calculation is built from the same handful of number-theory concepts.

items.name: Numbers
items.description: The set of two or more positive whole numbers being compared — this tool supports up to five at once.

items.name: Prime Factorization
items.description: A number written as a product of primes (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ...) — the unique "fingerprint" every whole number has, and the basis for computing both GCF and LCM.

items.name: Greatest Common Factor (GCF)
items.description: Also called the greatest common divisor (GCD) — the largest number that divides every number in the set with no remainder.

items.name: Least Common Multiple (LCM)
items.description: The smallest number that every number in the set divides into with no remainder.

examples.title: Worked Examples

applications.title: GCF & LCM in Practice
applications.intro: These two numbers show up any time equal-sized groups or recurring cycles need to line up exactly.

items.title: Adding and Simplifying Fractions
items.description: Adding fractions with different denominators requires a common denominator — the smallest one is the LCM of the denominators — and simplifying a fraction to lowest terms means dividing both numerator and denominator by their GCF.

items.title: Dividing Items into Equal Groups
items.description: Splitting several different-sized collections into the largest possible number of identical, evenly-filled groups (with nothing left over) uses the GCF of the collection sizes.

items.title: Scheduling Recurring Events
items.description: If one event repeats every m days and another every n days, the LCM of m and n gives the first day both happen again on the same day — the basis for planning shared schedules, shift rotations, or maintenance cycles.

items.title: Cryptography and Computer Science
items.description: The Euclidean algorithm for computing GCF is a core building block of RSA key generation and other cryptographic algorithms, and GCF/LCM logic appears throughout software that simplifies fractions, ratios, or timing intervals.

items.question: What's the actual difference between GCF and LCM?
items.answer: GCF is the largest number that divides evenly into every number in the set — it's always less than or equal to the smallest number given. LCM is the smallest number that every number in the set divides evenly into — it's always greater than or equal to the largest number given. They're opposite extremes of the same shared-factor relationship.

items.question: How does this work for more than two numbers?
items.answer: The GCF and LCM of three or more numbers can be found two at a time: compute GCF(a, b), then GCF of that result with c, and so on — the same works for LCM. This calculator applies that pairwise reduction automatically for however many numbers you enter.

items.question: Does this use the Euclidean algorithm?
items.answer: This tool finds GCF and LCM via prime factorization, which is easiest to follow and to show the work for. The Euclidean algorithm (repeated division with remainder) computes the same GCF more efficiently for very large numbers, without needing to factor them at all — both methods always agree.

items.question: Can the GCF of two numbers be 1?
items.answer: Yes — when two numbers share no prime factors at all (like 8 and 15), their GCF is 1 and they're called coprime or relatively prime. In that case their LCM is simply the two numbers multiplied together.

history.title: The Oldest Algorithm Still in Everyday Use
history.paragraph: The method for finding the greatest common factor of two numbers by repeated division — now called the Euclidean algorithm — appears in Book VII of Euclid's Elements, compiled around 300 BCE, making it one of the oldest algorithms still taught and used essentially unchanged today. Euclid presented it as a geometric procedure for finding the largest length that measures two given lengths evenly, but the same repeated-subtraction logic applies identically to whole numbers, which is how it's used now.

modernDevelopments.title: From Ancient Geometry to Modern Cryptography
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Euclid's algorithm turned out to have a life far beyond arithmetic: an extended version of it computes modular inverses, a step at the heart of the RSA public-key cryptosystem that secures much of the modern internet. Computer algebra systems and everyday software also lean on fast GCF computation to keep fractions and ratios in lowest terms automatically, making a 2,300-year-old procedure one of the most-executed algorithms in computing today.

conceptDiagram.title: What Pace Actually Measures
conceptDiagram.intro: Pace is the time spent covering one unit of distance. Between any two checkpoints on a route, it's simply the elapsed time divided by the distance covered since the last one — which is exactly what the Multipoint mode computes for real, uneven splits.
conceptDiagram.ariaLabel: A route with three checkpoints at 0 km / 0:00, 5 km / 25:00, and 10 km / 56:00, with the pace for each segment (5:00 per km, then 6:12 per km) labeled between the checkpoints
conceptDiagram.caption: Pace between two checkpoints = elapsed time ÷ distance covered

intro.title: Understanding Pace
intro.paragraph1: Pace is a rate expressed as time per unit of distance — minutes and seconds per kilometer or per mile — rather than distance per unit of time, which is what speed measures. The two describe the same motion from opposite directions: a pace of 5:00 per kilometer and a speed of 12 km/h are the same running effort, just expressed differently. Runners, walkers, and cyclists generally think in pace because it maps directly onto a training plan ("hold 5:00 per km for the middle three kilometers") and onto a finishing time (multiply pace by race distance), while speed is more common in cycling and motorized contexts.
intro.paragraph2: The underlying arithmetic is simple — pace = time ÷ distance, time = distance × pace, distance = time ÷ pace — but converting between a fixed pace and a finishing time by hand, across unit systems, and across race distances that aren't round numbers (a half marathon's 21.0975 km, a marathon's 42.195 km) is where a calculator earns its keep. This tool solves any one of pace, time, or distance from the other two, logs pace across multiple real checkpoints instead of assuming a constant effort for an entire run, converts pace between kilometers and miles directly, and projects a finishing time for a different distance from a result you've already run.

finishTimeFormula.title: Predicting a Finish Time
finishTimeFormula.paragraph1: A naive way to predict a longer race from a shorter one is to scale linearly: if you can hold a given pace for 10K, just multiply that time by 4.2195 to guess a marathon time. In practice this always predicts too fast a marathon, because endurance performance doesn't scale linearly with distance — pace predictably slows as an effort gets longer, due to fuel depletion, heat accumulation, and cumulative muscular fatigue that a short race never has time to expose.
finishTimeFormula.paragraph2: This tool instead uses the formula American research engineer and marathoner Peter Riegel published in Runner's World in 1977, and formalized the following distance-independent year in a 1981 paper for American Scientist: T₂ = T₁ × (D₂ ÷ D₁)^1.06. The exponent 1.06, derived by fitting the formula to a wide range of world-record and personal-best performances across running, walking, and swimming, is what captures that predictable slowdown — it's why the formula predicts a marathon time slower than simple linear scaling would, and why it's widely used (in a similar form) by race-prediction features in GPS running watches and training apps today. Riegel's own paper notes the formula holds best for efforts lasting between about 3.5 and 230 minutes, and gets less reliable for predictions across very different terrain, temperature, or training specificity — a 5K best predicts a marathon time only as well as your marathon-specific endurance actually matches your 5K speed.

applications.title: Where Pace Matters
applications.intro: Pace-based pacing is the standard way endurance sports are planned, coached, and raced.

items.title: Training plans
items.description: Structured running plans prescribe target paces for different workout types — easy runs, tempo runs, interval repeats — usually derived from a recent race result, so that each session trains a specific physiological system instead of just "running."

items.title: Race strategy
items.description: Even pacing (running each split at close to the same pace) is measurably more efficient than starting fast and slowing down, since a too-fast start burns limited glycogen reserves and accumulates fatigue faster than it can be recovered from later in the race — which is exactly what the Multipoint mode is built to check after the fact.

items.title: Course and event planning
items.description: Race organizers set course time limits and aid-station cutoffs from an assumed minimum pace, and GPS watches and pace bands (wristbands printed with a target split at each mile or kilometer) are built directly from a single target pace applied across an entire race distance.

items.question: What's the difference between pace and speed?
items.answer: They're the same underlying rate of motion expressed in inverse units. Pace is time per unit of distance (minutes per kilometer or mile) — smaller means faster. Speed is distance per unit of time (kilometers or miles per hour) — larger means faster. Converting between them is a division either way: speed = 60 ÷ pace-in-minutes-per-unit, and pace = 60 ÷ speed-in-units-per-hour.

items.question: Why does my pace change slightly when I switch between km and miles?
items.answer: It doesn't change your actual running speed — a mile (1.609344 km) is longer than a kilometer, so the same speed corresponds to a larger number of minutes per mile than per kilometer. A 5:00/km pace and an 8:03/mi pace describe the exact same speed, just measured against a different unit of distance.

items.question: How accurate is the Finish Time prediction?
items.answer: The Riegel formula is a well-established statistical fit across many athletes and distances, not a guarantee for any one individual race. It tends to be most accurate when the known and target distances are reasonably close and both efforts are run under similar conditions (terrain, weather, training state) — it will systematically over-predict how fast you can run a much longer distance if you haven't specifically trained your endurance for it.

items.question: What should I enter as checkpoints in the Multipoint mode?
items.answer: Cumulative distance and elapsed time measured from the very start of your run — the same numbers a GPS watch's mile or kilometer auto-lap alerts show, not the distance or time of each segment on its own. The tool subtracts each row from the one before it to compute the pace of that segment.

items.question: Why is the marathon world record pace so much slower than the 100 m record pace?
items.answer: Sprinting and endurance running draw on different physiological systems. A 100 m sprint is run almost entirely on stored ATP and creatine phosphate at a pace no runner could sustain for more than a few seconds, while a marathon is paced against the much slower rate at which the body can supply oxygen and fuel to muscles continuously for two hours — which is exactly the fatigue effect the Riegel exponent above is built to model.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: Pace as a concept is as old as measured racing itself — ancient Greek stadion races were already timed against a fixed, standardized distance. What's more recent is the mathematics of comparing effort across different distances. American research engineer and competitive marathoner Peter Riegel noticed that world-record times across running, walking, and swimming, plotted against their distances on a logarithmic scale, fell close to a single curve rather than a straight line — meaning record pace slows by a predictable, near-constant factor as distance increases, regardless of the sport. He first published the resulting time-versus-distance equation in Runner's World magazine in 1977, then formalized it academically in "Athletic Records and Human Endurance," American Scientist, 69(3), 285-290 (1981), giving endurance athletes and coaches a mathematical way to compare a runner's 10K performance against their marathon potential for the first time.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Consumer GPS watches (Garmin, Coros, Polar, and similar devices) now compute live pace every second from satellite positioning or a wrist-based accelerometer, and several running and cycling platforms build race-time predictors directly into their apps using a formula functionally equivalent to Riegel's. On the official-record side, world-record courses are certified against a physical, traceable calibration standard: a bicycle fitted with a Jones Counter, ridden along the exact course at least twice, per the measurement standard maintained jointly by World Athletics and the Association of International Marathons and Distance Races (AIMS) — the same certification process behind every marathon course record referenced in the table above.

quickReference.title: Common Random Draws
quickReference.intro: A few typical ranges and settings this generator is built to handle.

intro.title: Understanding Random Number Generation
intro.paragraph1: A computer can't produce a truly unpredictable number the way a physical dice roll or a coin flip does — every calculation a processor performs is deterministic, the same input always producing the same output. What this tool (and virtually every general-purpose random number feature in software) actually uses is a pseudorandom number generator: a deterministic algorithm that starts from an unpredictable seed value and produces a long sequence of numbers that pass statistical tests for randomness, even though the sequence is technically reproducible if the seed were known.
intro.paragraph2: Generating a random integer within a chosen range, without introducing bias toward any particular value, is less trivial than it sounds — naively taking a random value modulo the range size skews slightly toward smaller numbers unless the range divides evenly into the generator's output space. This tool avoids that bias, and when duplicates are disallowed, it draws without replacement by shuffling the full range rather than repeatedly re-rolling until a new value appears, which stays fast and uniform even as the requested count approaches the size of the range itself.

examples.title: Common Uses
examples.intro: The same generator, three different everyday settings.

rows.calculation: Picking a random winner from 250 entries

applications.title: Where Random Numbers Are Used
applications.intro: Beyond games of chance, random number generation is a foundational tool across many fields.

items.title: Statistical sampling
items.description: Selecting a random subset of a larger population — survey respondents, quality-control samples on a production line, or participants assigned to a study group — depends on random selection to avoid the bias a manually chosen sample would introduce.

items.title: Simulation and modeling
items.description: Monte Carlo simulations, used in fields from finance to physics, run a model thousands or millions of times with randomly varied inputs to estimate a range of possible outcomes rather than a single deterministic answer.

items.title: Randomized decisions and fairness
items.description: Assigning tasks, drawing raffle winners, shuffling a deck, or breaking ties fairly all rely on a source of randomness that no participant can predict or influence in advance.

items.question: Is this generator suitable for security purposes, like generating a password or encryption key?
items.answer: No. This tool uses a standard pseudorandom generator suited for everyday tasks like games, sampling, and simulations, not a cryptographically secure random number generator (CSPRNG). Security-sensitive values need a CSPRNG specifically, which resists an attacker predicting future output even after observing past output — a guarantee ordinary random number generators don't make.

items.question: Why can't I generate 10 unique numbers between 1 and 5?
items.answer: There are only 5 distinct whole numbers in that range, so it's mathematically impossible to draw 10 of them without repeating at least one. Disallowing duplicates caps the possible count at the size of the range itself.

items.question: Does the sort order change which numbers are generated?
items.answer: No. Sorting is applied only after the numbers are generated — it changes how the result is displayed, not which values were drawn or how likely any value was to appear.

items.question: Why do two different random number generators sometimes give different-feeling results for the same range?
items.answer: Different tools use different underlying pseudorandom algorithms and seeding methods, which affect the specific sequence produced (and how long it takes before that sequence repeats) even though both can be statistically valid sources of randomness for everyday use.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: Before computers could generate randomness algorithmically, researchers needed randomness that was demonstrably free of any hidden pattern for statistical work. In 1955, the RAND Corporation published "A Million Random Digits with 100,000 Normal Deviates," a book of a million random digits generated from an electronic roulette-wheel-like device and rigorously tested for statistical bias — for years, it was a standard reference source of randomness for researchers who needed it. The modern pseudorandom number generator emerged shortly after, as a way to produce comparably random-looking sequences algorithmically, on demand, without needing to consult a physical table.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The Mersenne Twister algorithm, published in 1998, became one of the most widely used general-purpose pseudorandom generators due to its extremely long period (before its output sequence repeats) and strong statistical properties, and remains the default generator in many programming languages and statistical tools today. For security-sensitive uses, modern systems instead rely on cryptographically secure generators seeded from genuine hardware entropy sources — thermal noise, timing jitter, or dedicated hardware random number generators built into modern CPUs — which browsers expose to web applications through the Web Crypto API specifically for that purpose.

quickReference.title: The Two Formulas
quickReference.intro: Population and sample standard deviation differ only in the denominator.

intro.title: Understanding Standard Deviation
intro.paragraph1: Standard deviation measures how spread out a set of values is around its mean — a small standard deviation means most values sit close to the average, while a large one means they're scattered widely. It's the square root of the variance, which itself is the average of each value's squared distance from the mean; squaring first (rather than just averaging the raw distances) ensures that deviations above and below the mean don't cancel each other out, and taking the square root at the end brings the result back to the data's original unit rather than a squared one.
intro.paragraph2: This tool computes both the population standard deviation (σ), used when your data set is the entire group you care about, and the sample standard deviation (s), used when your data is a subset drawn from a larger population you're trying to draw conclusions about. The two formulas differ only in the denominator — population divides by N, the sample divides by n − 1 — a small but deliberate adjustment called Bessel's correction, which corrects for the tendency of a sample's own mean to sit closer to its own data points than the true population mean would.

formula.title: The Formulas
formula.paragraph1: Both formulas start the same way: find the mean, subtract it from every value to get each value's deviation, then square each deviation (so negative and positive deviations both count as spread) and average them.
formula.paragraph2: σ is the population standard deviation and μ is the population mean, used when the data set is the entire group of interest. s is the sample standard deviation and x̄ is the sample mean, used when the data is only a subset of a larger population — dividing by n − 1 instead of n makes s a better (unbiased) estimate of the true population standard deviation than dividing by n would give.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few data sets, computed the same way this tool computes them.

applications.title: Where Standard Deviation Is Used
applications.intro: Standard deviation is one of the most widely used statistics because it quantifies uncertainty and consistency in a single number.

items.title: Quality control
items.description: Manufacturing processes track the standard deviation of a measured dimension or weight across a production run — a low standard deviation means the process is consistent, while a rising one often signals a machine going out of calibration before any single defective part is even produced.

items.title: Finance and risk
items.description: In finance, the standard deviation of an asset's historical returns is one of the most common measures of volatility — a higher standard deviation means returns swing more widely around their average, which is generally read as higher risk.

items.title: Grading and test design
items.description: Standardized test scores are typically reported alongside the test's standard deviation, since it tells you how meaningful a given point difference actually is — a 10-point gap matters far more on a test with a standard deviation of 15 than one with a standard deviation of 100.

items.question: Should I use population or sample standard deviation?
items.answer: Use population standard deviation (σ) only when your data set is genuinely the entire group you're interested in — every student in a specific class, every unit produced in a specific batch. Use sample standard deviation (s) whenever your data is a subset meant to represent a larger population you can't measure in full, which is the far more common situation in practice, including most surveys, experiments, and quality-control spot checks.

items.question: Why is the sample standard deviation always slightly larger than the population standard deviation for the same data?
items.answer: Because the sample formula divides the sum of squared deviations by a smaller number (n − 1 instead of n), which necessarily produces a larger result. This is deliberate: a sample's own mean is always at least as close to its own data points as any other value could be, which without correction would make the sample systematically underestimate the true spread of the population it was drawn from.

items.question: What does it mean if the standard deviation is 0?
items.answer: A standard deviation of exactly 0 means every value in the data set is identical — there's no spread at all, so every value equals the mean exactly.

items.question: How is standard deviation different from variance?
items.answer: Variance is the average of the squared deviations; standard deviation is simply its square root. Variance is expressed in squared units (which is mathematically convenient for further statistical calculations), while standard deviation is expressed in the same unit as the original data, which is usually easier to interpret directly.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The term "standard deviation" was coined by the English mathematician Karl Pearson, one of the founders of modern mathematical statistics, in a lecture in 1893 and in print the following year in his 1894 paper "Contributions to the Mathematical Theory of Evolution," published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Pearson introduced the term as a more convenient replacement for the older, more cumbersome phrases then in use, such as "error of mean square" and "root mean square error" — the underlying calculation itself had already been used by earlier statisticians and astronomers analyzing measurement error, but Pearson's terminology and systematic treatment are what stuck.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The n − 1 denominator used in the sample formula is known as Bessel's correction, after the German astronomer and mathematician Friedrich Bessel, who worked out the adjustment needed to remove the systematic bias that arises from estimating a population's spread using a sample's own mean rather than the population's true (and usually unknown) mean. Today, standard deviation calculations are built into essentially every statistical software package and spreadsheet application, and remain a foundational input to more advanced techniques including confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and control charts used throughout science, engineering, and business analytics.

quickReference.title: The Formulas
quickReference.intro: Every property of a circle follows from its radius alone.

intro.title: Understanding Circle Measurements
intro.paragraph1: A circle is fully defined by a single number: its radius, the distance from its center to any point on its edge. Every other common measurement — diameter, circumference, area — is a fixed multiple or function of that one radius, which is why knowing any one of the four measurements is always enough to recover the other three; there's no such thing as an "underdetermined" circle the way there can be for a general triangle or quadrilateral.
intro.paragraph2: The constant that links a circle's circumference to its diameter is π (pi) — an irrational number, roughly 3.14159, that never terminates or repeats in decimal form. Diameter is simply twice the radius; circumference is π times the diameter (equivalently, 2π times the radius); and area is π times the radius squared. This tool accepts whichever one of the four you already know and derives the rest instantly.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few common circle calculations, computed the same way this tool computes them.

applications.title: Where Circle Measurements Matter
applications.intro: Circular geometry shows up constantly in engineering, construction, and everyday measurement.

items.title: Engineering and manufacturing
items.description: Pipe diameters, gear radii, wheel circumferences, and the cross-sectional area of a cylindrical part are all circle measurements that directly determine flow capacity, mechanical fit, and material strength in countless manufactured components.

items.title: Construction and landscaping
items.description: Estimating the material needed for a circular garden bed, pool, or rounded architectural feature starts with converting between whichever dimension is easiest to measure on site (usually diameter or circumference with a tape measure) and the area needed to calculate material coverage.

items.title: Everyday estimation
items.description: Wrapping a circular object, fitting a round rug to a room, or comparing pizza sizes by diameter rather than price all come down to the same handful of circle relationships this tool computes.

items.question: Why is π an irrational number, and does that affect the accuracy of this calculator?
items.answer: π's digits never terminate or fall into a repeating pattern, so any calculation using it necessarily works with a rounded approximation. This tool uses your browser's built-in double-precision value of π (accurate to about 15-16 significant digits), which is far more precision than any real-world measurement could ever need or justify.

items.question: What's the difference between circumference and perimeter?
items.answer: They describe the same thing — the total distance around a shape's boundary — but "circumference" is the term used specifically for circles and other curved closed shapes, while "perimeter" is the general term used for any shape, including polygons with straight sides.

items.question: Can I enter a negative number or zero?
items.answer: No. A circle's radius, diameter, circumference, and area are all inherently positive quantities — a circle with zero or negative size isn't a meaningful circle, so this tool requires a positive value for whichever measurement you provide.

items.question: How do I find the area of a circle if I only know its circumference?
items.answer: First divide the circumference by 2π to get the radius, then square that radius and multiply by π to get the area — exactly the two-step conversion this tool performs automatically when you select "Circumference" as your known value.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The relationship between a circle's circumference and its diameter was studied across many ancient civilizations, but the first rigorous mathematical method for bounding its value came from the Greek mathematician Archimedes of Syracuse around 250 BCE, in his treatise "Measurement of a Circle." Archimedes inscribed and circumscribed regular polygons with up to 96 sides around a circle, using the polygons' known perimeters to trap the true value of what we now call π between two close bounds — proving it fell between 3+10/71 and 3+1/7, a result accurate to two decimal places that stood as the best-known approximation for centuries.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Modern computers, using algorithms like the Chudnovsky algorithm (based on a rapidly converging series discovered by the Chudnovsky brothers in 1989), have calculated π to over 100 trillion decimal digits — a scale with no practical engineering use (NASA's most demanding calculations, like plotting interplanetary trajectories, need fewer than 20 digits), but which serves as a demanding real-world stress test for supercomputer hardware and serves ongoing research into the still-unproven question of whether π's digits are truly statistically random.

quickReference.title: The Formulas
quickReference.intro: Every triangle-solving mode reduces to the Law of Cosines or the Law of Sines.

intro.title: Understanding Triangle Solving
intro.paragraph1: A triangle has six measurements — three sides and three angles — but only three of them, in the right combination, are needed to pin down the whole shape. "Solving" a triangle means starting from three known measurements and deriving the other three, along with derived quantities like area and perimeter. The four combinations that always determine a unique triangle are known by the shorthand SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the angle between them), ASA (two angles and the side between them), and AAS (two angles and a side not between them).
intro.paragraph2: Two classical relationships do all the work: the Law of Cosines, which generalizes the Pythagorean theorem to any triangle (not just right triangles) and is used whenever a full set of sides or an included angle is known, and the Law of Sines, which relates each side to the sine of its opposite angle and is used whenever two angles are already known. This calculator picks whichever law fits the combination of inputs you provide, then checks the result against the triangle inequality (any two sides must outweigh the third) and the fact that every triangle's angles sum to exactly 180°.

modes.title: The Four Solving Modes
modes.intro: Each mode corresponds to a different combination of three known measurements.

items.title: SSS — Side-Side-Side
items.description: All three side lengths are known. The Law of Cosines derives each angle in turn from the three sides; this is the only mode where the triangle's size and shape are both fully fixed by the input alone.

items.title: SAS — Side-Angle-Side
items.description: Two sides and the angle trapped between them are known. The Law of Cosines finds the third side directly from that angle, after which the remaining angles follow the same way as in SSS.

items.title: ASA — Angle-Side-Angle
items.description: Two angles and the side between them are known. The third angle follows immediately since all three must sum to 180°, and the Law of Sines then scales the other two sides to match the known side.

items.title: AAS — Angle-Angle-Side
items.description: Two angles and a side that is not between them are known. This solves identically to ASA once the third angle is found (the same Law of Sines ratio applies), which is why AAS and ASA always produce the same kind of unique solution.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few classic triangles solved the same way this tool solves them.

items.question: Why do I need exactly three measurements, not two or four?
items.answer: Two measurements leave a triangle's shape ambiguous — infinitely many triangles can share, say, just two side lengths. Four or more measurements are usually over-determined and can be mutually inconsistent (they might not describe any real triangle at all). Three measurements, in one of the four valid combinations, are both necessary and sufficient to fix a triangle uniquely.

items.question: What happens if I enter values that can't form a real triangle?
items.answer: This tool checks two hard rules: the triangle inequality (the sum of any two sides must exceed the third — otherwise the sides are too short to meet and close the shape) and the angle sum rule (a triangle's three angles must always add up to exactly 180°). If either rule is broken, it reports that no valid triangle exists rather than showing a misleading result.

items.question: Why doesn't this tool support SSA (side-side-angle)?
items.answer: SSA is deliberately left out because it's ambiguous: unlike the other four combinations, a given set of two sides and a non-included angle can correspond to zero, one, or two different valid triangles (the well-known "ambiguous case" from trigonometry), so it doesn't reliably determine a single answer the way SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAS do.

items.question: How accurate are the results?
items.answer: Calculations use double-precision floating-point trigonometry, accurate to roughly 15 significant digits — far beyond what any physical measurement could need. Results are rounded for display, but the underlying area, perimeter, and angle values are computed at full precision.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: Triangle-solving methods trace back to ancient Babylonian and Egyptian surveying, but their systematic mathematical treatment began with Greek geometers, especially Euclid's Elements (c. 300 BCE), which proved the angle-sum and side-length relationships this tool relies on. The Law of Sines and Law of Cosines themselves were developed more fully by Islamic Golden Age mathematicians and astronomers — notably Al-Battani and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi in the 9th–13th centuries — who needed precise spherical and planar triangle solutions for astronomical calculations and were the first to treat trigonometry as a subject independent of astronomy.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The same triangle-solving relationships now underpin GPS positioning (which triangulates a receiver's location from satellite distances), computer graphics (where every 3D surface is approximated by a mesh of triangles that must be measured and rendered efficiently), and structural engineering, where triangular trusses are analyzed using exactly these side-and-angle relationships because a triangle is the only polygon whose shape is rigidly fixed by its side lengths alone.

quickReference.title: The Formulas
quickReference.intro: Every probability rule builds on the same basic favorable-over-total ratio.

intro.title: Understanding Probability
intro.paragraph1: Probability measures how likely an event is to happen, expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain) — or, equivalently, between 0% and 100%. For a single event with equally likely outcomes, probability is simply the count of favorable outcomes divided by the total count of possible outcomes: rolling a 3 on a fair six-sided die has probability 1/6, because exactly one of the six equally likely faces is a 3.
intro.paragraph2: Real situations usually involve more than one event, which is where the rules for combining probabilities come in. The AND rule multiplies two independent probabilities together to find the chance both happen. The OR rule adds two probabilities and subtracts their overlap, so shared outcomes aren't counted twice. Conditional probability narrows the field to only the outcomes where a condition is already known to be true, then asks how likely the event is within that narrower set. This calculator implements all four relationships directly from their standard definitions.

modes.title: The Four Calculation Modes
modes.intro: Each mode answers a different kind of probability question.

items.title: Single Event
items.description: The simplest case: given a number of favorable outcomes out of a total number of equally likely outcomes, this mode returns the probability, its percentage form, and the equivalent betting-odds notation (odds for and against).

items.title: A and B (Independent Events)
items.description: Finds the probability that two independent events — where one event's outcome has no effect on the other's — both occur, by multiplying their individual probabilities together. Independence is the key assumption: this rule does not apply to events that influence each other.

items.title: A or B (Union of Events)
items.description: Finds the probability that at least one of two events occurs, by adding their individual probabilities and subtracting the probability that both occur together (to avoid double-counting the overlap). Entering 0 for the "both" probability correctly handles mutually exclusive events that can never happen at the same time.

items.title: A given B (Conditional Probability)
items.description: Finds the probability of event A occurring, restricted to only the scenarios where event B is already known to have happened, by dividing the probability of both occurring together by the probability of B alone. This is the mathematical basis for updating a probability estimate in light of new information.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few classic probability questions, computed the same way this tool computes them.

rows.calculation: Rolling a 3 on a fair die (1 of 6 outcomes)
Two coin flips both landing heads
Drawing a king or a heart from a deck

items.question: What's the difference between probability and odds?
items.answer: Probability is favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes (a fraction of the whole, from 0 to 1). Odds compare favorable outcomes directly to unfavorable outcomes (a ratio of the two, like "5 to 1"). They describe the same underlying chance, just in two different, commonly used formats — this calculator's single-event mode reports both.

items.question: Why does the AND rule only work for independent events?
items.answer: The AND rule (multiplying probabilities) assumes one event's outcome doesn't change the other event's probability at all. If the events are dependent — like drawing two cards from a deck without replacement, where the first draw changes what's left for the second — this simple multiplication gives the wrong answer, and conditional probability must be used instead.

items.question: Why do I subtract the overlap in the OR rule?
items.answer: Adding two probabilities directly counts any outcome that satisfies both events twice — once in each probability. Subtracting the probability that both happen together removes that double-count, leaving the correct probability that at least one of the two events occurs.

items.question: Can a probability be negative or greater than 100%?
items.answer: No. Probability is fundamentally bounded between 0% (the event never happens) and 100% (the event always happens), since it represents a fraction of all possible outcomes. This calculator rejects any input that would produce a value outside that range as invalid.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The formal mathematical study of probability began in 1654 with a correspondence between French mathematicians Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat, prompted by a gambler's question about how to fairly divide the stakes of an interrupted dice game. Their exchange of letters worked out the first rigorous rules for combining probabilities of separate events — laying the foundation, decades later, for what Pierre-Simon Laplace would formalize as classical probability theory in his 1812 treatise "Théorie Analytique des Probabilités."

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: In 1933, Soviet mathematician Andrey Kolmogorov placed probability on a rigorous axiomatic foundation using measure theory, unifying centuries of separate results (including the AND, OR, and conditional rules this calculator implements) into a single consistent framework still used today. Modern applications built on these same rules span medical diagnostic testing (interpreting what a positive test result actually implies via conditional probability), machine learning classifiers, insurance risk pricing, and the statistical methods behind nearly all scientific research.

result.emptyDataset: Enter at least one value to see a result.

quickReference.title: The Formulas
quickReference.intro: Four different ways of summarizing a data set with a single number.

intro.title: Understanding Central Tendency and Spread
intro.paragraph1: Mean, median, and mode are the three most common "measures of central tendency" — different ways of summarizing an entire data set with one representative number. Range, by contrast, is a measure of spread: it says how far the data stretches, not where its center is. Together these four numbers give a quick statistical snapshot of a data set without needing to look at every individual value.
intro.paragraph2: The mean (the everyday "average") is the sum of all values divided by how many there are. The median is the middle value when the data is sorted from smallest to largest — the halfway point of the ordered data, found by averaging the two middle values when there's an even count. The mode is whichever value (or values) appears most often; if every value is unique, there is no mode at all. The range is simply the largest value minus the smallest.

measures.title: The Four Measures
measures.intro: Each measure captures something different about the same data set.

items.title: Mean
items.description: The arithmetic average — sum every value and divide by the count. The mean uses every single value in the data set, which makes it sensitive to outliers: one extremely large or small value can pull it noticeably away from where most of the data actually sits.

items.title: Median
items.description: The middle value once the data is sorted. Because it only depends on the position of values, not their exact size, the median is far more resistant to outliers than the mean — a useful property whenever a data set might contain unusually large or small values, like household incomes or home prices.

items.title: Mode
items.description: The most frequently occurring value. Unlike mean and median, the mode can be used on non-numeric categorical data (like "favorite color"), and a data set can have one mode, several modes (if multiple values tie for most frequent), or no mode at all (if every value appears exactly once).

items.title: Range
items.description: The difference between the largest and smallest values — the simplest possible measure of how spread out a data set is. It's easy to compute but, since it depends on only the two most extreme values, a single outlier can make the range far larger than what most of the data actually looks like.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few data sets and what this calculator returns for each.

items.question: When should I use the median instead of the mean?
items.answer: Use the median whenever a data set might contain extreme outliers that would skew the mean, such as income, home prices, or response times. A famous example: adding one billionaire to a room of a hundred people barely moves the median income but sends the mean income soaring, since the mean is pulled toward extreme values while the median is not.

items.question: Can a data set have more than one mode?
items.answer: Yes. A data set is called "bimodal" if exactly two values tie for the highest frequency, or "multimodal" more generally if three or more values tie. This calculator reports every value that ties for the highest frequency, in ascending order.

items.question: Why does a data set sometimes have no mode?
items.answer: The mode only exists when at least one value repeats more often than the others. If every value in the data set appears exactly once, no value stands out as "most frequent," so by convention there is no mode at all — rather than treating every unique value as equally the mode.

items.question: How is the median calculated when there's an even number of values?
items.answer: Sort the data, then take the two values that sit in the middle and average them. For example, in {2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 8} (6 values), the two middle values after sorting are 5 and 6, so the median is (5+6)/2 = 5.5.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The arithmetic mean has been used since antiquity for tasks like dividing goods fairly, but the median and mode as formal statistical concepts emerged much later. The term "median" in this statistical sense was popularized by Francis Galton in the 1880s, who favored it for its resistance to outliers when studying inherited traits, while the term "mode" was introduced by Karl Pearson in 1895 as part of his broader effort to formalize descriptive statistics — the branch of statistics concerned with summarizing data sets, as opposed to drawing inferences from them.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: These four measures remain foundational to modern data analysis: they're typically the very first calculations run on any new data set, whether in scientific research, business analytics, or machine learning preprocessing (where the choice between mean and median for handling missing values, for example, can meaningfully change a model's behavior). Interactive dashboards and business intelligence tools compute all four automatically and continuously as new data arrives, making them the most-computed statistics in day-to-day data work worldwide.
