quickReference.title: The Formulas
quickReference.intro: Every training zone is a percentage band of your estimated maximum heart rate.

intro.title: Understanding Target Heart Rate
intro.paragraph1: Target heart rate zones translate exercise intensity into a heart rate range you can monitor in real time, so you can train at a specific effort level rather than guessing. The starting point is your estimated maximum heart rate — the fastest your heart can safely beat during maximal exertion — from which five standard training zones are calculated as percentage bands, from very light activity up to maximum effort.
intro.paragraph2: This calculator estimates maximum heart rate using the classic "220 minus age" formula, still the most widely cited estimate despite being a population average that can be off by 10-20 beats per minute for any specific individual. When you also provide your resting heart rate, it switches to the Karvonen method, which calculates zones from your heart rate reserve (max minus resting) instead of straight percentages of max — a more personalized estimate, since it accounts for your current fitness level rather than treating everyone the same age as identical.

zones.title: The Five Training Zones
zones.intro: Each zone corresponds to a different training goal and physiological effect.

items.title: Very Light (50-60%)
items.description: Warm-up and cool-down intensity, and the zone most associated with active recovery between harder sessions. Easy enough to sustain a full conversation without noticing your breathing.

items.title: Light (60-70%)
items.description: Often called the "fat-burning zone" because a higher percentage of calories burned at this intensity come from fat versus carbohydrates — though total calories burned per minute is lower than in harder zones, so it isn't necessarily the fastest way to burn fat overall.

items.title: Moderate (70-80%)
items.description: The classic aerobic or "cardio" zone, widely recommended as the target for building cardiovascular endurance. Breathing noticeably deepens and holding a conversation becomes difficult.

items.title: Hard (80-90%)
items.description: The anaerobic threshold zone, where the body starts relying more heavily on energy systems that don't require oxygen. Used for interval training and building speed and performance rather than pure endurance.

items.title: Maximum (90-100%)
items.description: Near-maximal to maximal effort, sustainable only for short bursts. Used sparingly in interval training by well-conditioned athletes, and generally not a zone to train in continuously.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few ages and what this calculator returns for each.

items.question: How accurate is the "220 minus age" formula?
items.answer: It's a population-average estimate derived from studies in the 1970s, and for any specific individual the true maximum heart rate can differ from this estimate by 10-20 beats per minute in either direction. It remains useful as a general guide for setting training zones, but a supervised maximal exercise test is the only way to know your actual maximum heart rate precisely.

items.question: Why does adding my resting heart rate change the zones?
items.answer: The Karvonen method calculates zones as a percentage of your heart rate reserve (max heart rate minus resting heart rate) rather than a percentage of max heart rate alone. Two people with the same max heart rate but different fitness levels — and therefore different resting heart rates — will get different, more personalized target zones with this method.

items.question: What's a normal resting heart rate?
items.answer: Most adults have a resting heart rate between 60 and 100 beats per minute, measured after several minutes of rest, ideally first thing in the morning before getting out of bed. Well-conditioned athletes often have resting heart rates well below 60, sometimes in the 40s, reflecting a more efficient heart.

items.question: Should I always train in the "fat-burning" zone to lose weight?
items.answer: Not necessarily. While the light zone burns a higher percentage of calories from fat, total calorie burn (and therefore total fat burned) per minute is generally higher in more intense zones, since more overall energy is being expended. Total calories burned over time tends to matter more for weight loss than which specific fuel source is used minute to minute.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The "220 minus age" formula for estimating maximum heart rate traces back to a 1971 review by physiologist William Haskell and cardiologist Samuel Fox, who summarized existing (and largely unpublished) data into what became the most commonly cited estimate in exercise science. Heart rate training zones themselves grew out of research into aerobic exercise physiology in the 1960s and 70s, as sports scientists sought objective, measurable ways to prescribe and monitor exercise intensity beyond a person's own subjective sense of effort.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Subsequent research has produced more refined maximum heart rate formulas — such as the Tanaka formula (208 minus 0.7 times age), published in 2001 from a meta-analysis of over 18,000 subjects — that tend to be more accurate for older adults, though "220 minus age" remains the most widely used in consumer fitness devices. Modern wearables and fitness trackers now measure heart rate continuously via optical sensors, letting athletes monitor their real-time zone during a workout rather than relying on the estimate alone, and some devices further refine zone estimates using a lab-measured or field-tested maximum heart rate instead of an age-based formula.

quickReference.title: The Math
quickReference.intro: Every suggested time is built from whole 90-minute sleep cycles.

intro.title: Understanding Sleep Cycles
intro.paragraph1: Sleep isn't a single uniform state — it moves through a repeating cycle of distinct stages roughly every 90 minutes throughout the night, and waking up in the middle of a cycle (particularly during deep sleep) tends to produce the groggy, disoriented feeling known as sleep inertia. Waking up at the boundary between two cycles, when sleep is naturally lighter, is the popular heuristic behind sleep-cycle calculators like this one.
intro.paragraph2: This calculator works in whole 90-minute cycles, adding a short buffer (adjustable, defaulting to 15 minutes) for the time it typically takes to actually fall asleep after getting into bed. Given a target wake-up time, it counts backward in full cycles to suggest bedtimes; given a bedtime, it counts forward to suggest wake-up times. Either way, it offers a range from 6 cycles (9 hours of sleep) down to 3 cycles (4.5 hours), since needs and schedules vary — 6 cycles is the option most aligned with standard sleep recommendations for adults.

stages.title: The Stages Within Each Cycle
stages.intro: A single 90-minute sleep cycle moves through several distinct stages.

items.title: Light Sleep (Stages 1-2)
items.description: The transition into sleep and the largest share of total sleep time. Heart rate and breathing slow, body temperature drops, and it's the stage most people wake from feeling relatively alert.

items.title: Deep Sleep (Stage 3)
items.description: Also called slow-wave sleep, concentrated in the earlier cycles of the night. This is when the body does most of its physical repair work — tissue growth, muscle repair, and immune system reinforcement — and waking from it produces the most severe grogginess.

items.title: REM Sleep
items.description: The stage most associated with vivid dreaming, where brain activity resembles wakefulness even though the body is briefly paralyzed. REM periods lengthen with each successive cycle through the night, making the later cycles increasingly REM-dominant.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few schedules and what this calculator returns for each.

items.question: Is 90 minutes an exact, universal sleep cycle length?
items.answer: No — 90 minutes is a commonly cited average, but actual sleep cycle length varies by individual and even from night to night for the same person, typically ranging from about 70 to 120 minutes. This calculator uses the widely adopted 90-minute average as a practical estimate, not a personalized, measured value.

items.question: Why does the calculator suggest a range of options instead of one time?
items.answer: Different numbers of completed cycles suit different situations — 6 cycles (9 hours) aligns with standard adult sleep recommendations, while fewer cycles might fit a night with an early morning commitment. Showing several cycle-aligned options lets you pick the one that best fits your schedule, rather than a single rigid answer.

items.question: Why does it add extra minutes for falling asleep?
items.answer: The cycle math starts counting from the moment you actually fall asleep, not the moment you get into bed — most people take a certain number of minutes to drift off after lying down. Accounting for this buffer keeps the suggested clock times realistic rather than assuming instant sleep onset.

items.question: Does waking up between cycles guarantee I'll feel rested?
items.answer: It can help reduce sleep inertia (grogginess from waking mid-cycle), but total sleep duration, sleep quality, consistency of schedule, and individual factors like stress and health all matter at least as much. Cycle-timed wake-ups are a helpful heuristic, not a guarantee of feeling fully rested.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The cyclical, stage-based structure of sleep was first identified through overnight brain-wave recordings by physiologist Nathaniel Kleitman and his student Eugene Aserinsky at the University of Chicago, whose 1953 discovery of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep revealed that sleep was not a single uniform state but a recurring cycle of distinct stages. Kleitman's subsequent research established the roughly 90-minute period of this cycle, now known as the basic rest-activity cycle, as a foundational concept in sleep science.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Modern sleep tracking, from clinical polysomnography (which measures brain waves, eye movement, and muscle activity directly) to consumer wearables (which infer sleep stages indirectly from movement and heart rate), has refined understanding of individual variation in cycle length and stage proportions well beyond the original 90-minute average. Sleep-cycle calculators like this one remain a popular, accessible heuristic precisely because they require no special equipment — just a target time and the well-established average cycle length — even though a lab sleep study remains the only way to measure an individual's actual cycle structure precisely.

quickReference.title: The Formula
quickReference.intro: The US Navy method estimates body fat from circumference measurements alone.

intro.title: Understanding the US Navy Body Fat Method
intro.paragraph1: Body fat percentage — the proportion of total body weight that is fat tissue, as opposed to muscle, bone, organs, and water — is a more direct measure of body composition than BMI, which cannot distinguish a muscular body from a fat one at the same height and weight. The US Navy method estimates it from a small set of tape-measure circumferences (neck, waist, and for women, hip) rather than skinfold calipers, DEXA scans, or underwater weighing, trading some precision for a measurement almost anyone can take at home with just a tape measure.
intro.paragraph2: The formula, developed by Hodgdon and Beckett in 1984 for the US Navy's body composition standards, uses the logarithm of these circumference measurements because body fat's relationship to circumference isn't linear — small waist changes matter more at some body sizes than others, and the logarithmic form captures that curve better than a simple ratio would. Men's and women's formulas differ because fat distribution patterns differ meaningfully by sex, on average, which is also why the method requires a hip measurement for women but not for men.

categoriesSection.title: The Five Body Fat Categories
categoriesSection.intro: This tool classifies results using the American Council on Exercise (ACE) categories, which differ by gender because women naturally carry a higher essential-fat percentage.

items.title: Essential Fat
items.description: The minimum body fat needed for basic physiological function — hormone production, organ protection, and vitamin storage. Sustained levels at or below this floor are associated with health risks, not fitness gains.

items.title: Athletes
items.description: The range typically seen in competitive athletes, reflecting low body fat maintained through high training volume, though not necessarily a target appropriate or sustainable for the general population.

items.title: Fitness
items.description: A lean, fit range achievable and maintainable through regular exercise and typical healthy-eating habits, without the extreme training volume associated with the athletes category.

items.title: Average
items.description: The range most adults in the general population fall into — associated with typical, moderate health risk, neither notably lean nor at an elevated-risk level.

items.title: Obese
items.description: Body fat levels associated with meaningfully elevated risk for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and other metabolic conditions, independent of the additional information BMI or weight alone would provide.

examples.title: Worked Examples

items.question: How accurate is the US Navy circumference method?
items.answer: Compared to gold-standard methods like DEXA scans or hydrostatic weighing, the US Navy method typically has an error margin of around 3-4 percentage points, which is generally considered acceptable for tracking trends over time even though it isn't as precise as lab-based measurement. Consistent measurement technique (same tape tension, same body positions, same time of day) matters more for tracking change than the method's absolute accuracy.

items.question: Why does the formula need a hip measurement for women but not for men?
items.answer: On average, women carry proportionally more fat in the hip and thigh area (a "gynoid" distribution pattern) while men tend to carry more around the abdomen (an "android" pattern). The original US Navy research found that including hip circumference substantially improved the formula's accuracy for women specifically, while it added no meaningful accuracy for men.

items.question: Where exactly should I measure my waist and neck?
items.answer: Measure the neck circumference just below the larynx (Adam's apple), with the tape sloping slightly downward toward the front. Measure the waist at the level of the navel while standing relaxed (not sucking in), and for women, measure the hip at its widest point. Keep the tape measure snug against the skin without compressing it for an accurate reading.

items.question: Why is body fat percentage more useful than BMI for some purposes?
items.answer: BMI is calculated purely from height and weight, so it can't distinguish between a heavily muscled person and a person carrying excess fat at the same BMI value — a well-known limitation, especially for athletes. Body fat percentage measures body composition more directly, which is why it's often used alongside BMI rather than as a full replacement for it.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The US Navy circumference method was developed in 1984 by researchers James Hodgdon and Michael Beckett at the Naval Health Research Center, tasked with finding a body composition standard for military fitness assessment that was more accurate than height-weight tables but far more practical in the field than skinfold calipers or laboratory methods. Their research validated the formula against hydrostatic (underwater) weighing, the reference standard for body composition measurement at the time, across a large sample of Navy personnel.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The method remains in active use across the US military services today for periodic body composition assessment, valued precisely because it requires no special equipment beyond a tape measure. In civilian fitness and research contexts, it has since been compared extensively against newer reference methods like DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) scans, which confirm its reasonable accuracy for population-level and trend tracking, while more precise imaging-based methods remain preferred for clinical or research applications requiring higher precision.

quickReference.title: The Formulas
quickReference.intro: Every method ultimately estimates a conception date, then adds the standard 266-day gestation period.

intro.title: Understanding Due Date Estimation
intro.paragraph1: A due date is an estimate, not a prediction with pinpoint accuracy — only about 5% of babies are actually born on their calculated due date, with the large majority arriving anywhere within two weeks before or after it. Despite that inherent uncertainty, an estimated due date remains a clinically essential anchor point: it's used to time prenatal screening tests, track fetal growth against expected milestones, and decide when a pregnancy is considered "full term" versus early or late.
intro.paragraph2: Pregnancy is conventionally measured in "gestational age," counted from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP) rather than from the actual date of conception — even though conception typically happens about two weeks after that date. This convention exists simply because the LMP date is usually known with confidence, while the exact conception date rarely is. A full-term pregnancy is defined as 280 days (40 weeks) from the LMP, which is equivalent to 266 days (38 weeks) from conception itself.

methods.title: The Four Calculation Methods
methods.intro: Each method anchors the estimate to whichever date you actually know with confidence.

items.title: Last Menstrual Period (Naegele's Rule)
items.description: The most common method: adds 280 days to the first day of the last period. Originally described assuming a standard 28-day cycle with ovulation on day 14, this calculator adjusts the estimate for a different average cycle length by shifting the assumed ovulation day accordingly.

items.title: Conception Date
items.description: If the conception date is known precisely (for example, from ovulation tracking), 266 days are added directly to it — skipping the LMP-based estimate of when ovulation occurred, since the actual date is already known.

items.title: IVF 3-Day Transfer
items.description: In IVF, the embryo's exact age is known precisely at the moment of transfer. A 3-day-old embryo (cleavage stage) is already 3 days past conception, so only 263 more days (266 minus 3) are added to the transfer date.

items.title: IVF 5-Day Transfer
items.description: A 5-day-old embryo (blastocyst stage) is 5 days past conception at transfer, so only 261 more days (266 minus 5) are added — IVF due dates are generally considered the most precise of the four methods, since both the embryo's age and the transfer date are known exactly.

items.question: How accurate is a calculated due date?
items.answer: Due dates estimated this way are a statistical average, not a precise prediction — most healthy pregnancies deliver anywhere within about two weeks before or after the calculated date, and only a small fraction of births land exactly on it. An early ultrasound (typically in the first trimester) can refine the estimate based on measured fetal size, which is often considered more accurate than an LMP-based calculation alone, especially for irregular cycles.

items.question: Why is pregnancy measured from the last period instead of conception?
items.answer: The last menstrual period date is almost always known with confidence, while the exact date of conception (fertilization) is rarely known precisely, since it can happen anywhere within the several-day fertile window around ovulation. Counting from a reliably known date, even though it precedes actual conception by about two weeks, makes gestational age a consistent, comparable measure across pregnancies.

items.question: What's considered "full term"?
items.answer: Full term is conventionally defined as 39 weeks 0 days through 40 weeks 6 days of gestational age. Babies born from 37 weeks 0 days to 38 weeks 6 days are considered "early term," and those born before 37 weeks are considered preterm — these distinctions matter clinically because outcomes and typical care differ across these windows.

items.question: Why does a longer cycle length shift the due date later?
items.answer: In a longer cycle, ovulation (and therefore conception) tends to happen later relative to the start of the period, since the follicular phase before ovulation varies more in length than the luteal phase after it. Since gestational age is counted from the LMP regardless, a later actual conception means the same LMP date corresponds to a later true due date.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The convention of adding 280 days to the last menstrual period is widely known as Naegele's rule, after German obstetrician Franz Karl Naegele, who described it in his 1830 textbook on obstetrics. Naegele himself credited the underlying idea to earlier observations, including work by Swedish obstetrician Peter Alexander Wibom, but Naegele's clear formulation became the version that persisted in medical education and practice for nearly two centuries.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Modern research has scrutinized the assumptions behind Naegele's rule, including a widely cited study by Jukic and colleagues in 2013, which found the average pregnancy actually lasted closer to 268 days from ovulation for first-time mothers (versus the 266 the classic rule assumes) with substantial individual variation. Modern obstetric practice now typically combines LMP-based dating with first-trimester ultrasound measurements of fetal crown-rump length, which research has shown provides a more accurate due date estimate than LMP alone, particularly for people with irregular cycles or uncertain LMP dates.

quickReference.title: The Formula
quickReference.intro: Ovulation is estimated backward from the next expected period, not forward from the last one.

intro.title: Understanding Ovulation and the Fertile Window
intro.paragraph1: Ovulation is the release of a mature egg from an ovary, the single event in the menstrual cycle when pregnancy becomes possible. Because the egg survives for only about 24 hours after release, and sperm can survive in the reproductive tract for up to about 5 days, the "fertile window" — the days when intercourse can result in pregnancy — spans roughly the 5 days before ovulation through the day after it, even though conception itself can only happen on ovulation day.
intro.paragraph2: A key insight behind estimating ovulation from cycle length is that the menstrual cycle has two phases of unequal consistency: the follicular phase (from the start of the period to ovulation) varies considerably in length from person to person and cycle to cycle, while the luteal phase (from ovulation to the next period) is remarkably consistent, typically 12-14 days regardless of overall cycle length. This is why this calculator estimates ovulation by counting backward a fixed number of days from the next expected period, rather than counting forward a fixed number of days from the last one.

phases.title: The Phases of the Menstrual Cycle
phases.intro: Each phase is governed by a different balance of reproductive hormones.

items.title: Menstrual Phase
items.description: The shedding of the uterine lining, marking day 1 of the cycle. Typically lasts 3-7 days, though this varies by individual.

items.title: Follicular Phase
items.description: Runs from day 1 until ovulation, during which follicles in the ovary mature under the influence of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and the uterine lining rebuilds. This is the phase most responsible for overall cycle length variability.

items.title: Ovulation
items.description: Triggered by a surge in luteinizing hormone (LH), a mature egg is released from the dominant follicle. This single-day event is the only point in the cycle when fertilization can occur.

items.title: Luteal Phase
items.description: Runs from ovulation to the start of the next period. The ruptured follicle transforms into the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone to prepare the uterine lining for a potential pregnancy. Its length is remarkably consistent, which is why it anchors this calculator's backward-counting method.

items.question: How accurate is an ovulation estimate based on cycle length alone?
items.answer: It's a useful starting estimate, especially for people with regular cycles, but it can't account for cycle-to-cycle variation that affects almost everyone to some degree. Tracking methods that observe direct physical signals — basal body temperature, cervical mucus changes, or urine LH test strips — generally provide more precise, real-time confirmation of ovulation than a calendar estimate alone.

items.question: Why does this calculator project three cycles instead of just one?
items.answer: Showing the next few cycles helps illustrate the pattern and gives a practical planning window beyond just the immediate cycle, which is useful whether the goal is trying to conceive or avoiding pregnancy. Each projected cycle uses the same average cycle length assumption, so accuracy for cycles further in the future depends on how consistent an individual's actual cycle length is.

items.question: What if my cycles are irregular?
items.answer: This calculator's estimates are least reliable for irregular cycles, since it assumes a consistent average cycle length. In that case, direct fertility tracking methods (basal body temperature charting, ovulation predictor kits, or cervical mucus monitoring) are considerably more useful than calendar-based calculations, and a healthcare provider can help investigate the cause of irregularity if it's a persistent concern.

items.question: Can I get pregnant on any day of my cycle?
items.answer: No — pregnancy can only result from intercourse during the fertile window, roughly the 5 days before ovulation through the day after it, because that's the only period when both a viable egg and viable sperm can be present simultaneously in the reproductive tract. Outside that window, conception is not possible regardless of when intercourse occurs.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: Understanding of ovulation timing advanced significantly in the 1920s through the independent work of Japanese gynecologist Kyusaku Ogino and Austrian gynecologist Hermann Knaus, who each separately established that ovulation occurs at a predictable interval before the next menstrual period, rather than at a fixed interval after the last one. Their calendar-based insight, now known as the Ogino-Knaus method, became the scientific foundation for the rhythm method of natural family planning and remains the conceptual basis for how ovulation calculators like this one estimate timing today.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Modern fertility tracking has moved well beyond calendar calculations alone, incorporating basal body temperature monitoring (which rises slightly after ovulation due to progesterone), urine test strips that detect the LH surge directly 24-36 hours before ovulation, and consumer wearables that track multiple physiological signals continuously. Research comparing these methods consistently shows that direct hormonal or physiological tracking provides more precise, individualized ovulation timing than calendar-based calculation alone, which is best used as a general planning estimate rather than a precise prediction.

intro.title: Understanding Week-by-Week Pregnancy Tracking
intro.paragraph1: This tracker follows a pregnancy's progress in "gestational age" — time counted from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP), the standard convention used throughout obstetric care, even though actual conception typically occurs about two weeks after that date. A full-term pregnancy spans 40 weeks (280 days) of gestational age, divided into three trimesters of roughly 13-14 weeks each, each associated with distinct stages of fetal development and different typical experiences for the pregnant person.
intro.paragraph2: Alongside the numeric gestational age, this tracker includes a weekly size comparison — the popular "your baby is about the size of a lemon" style of milestone that many pregnancy trackers use to make fetal growth more tangible than a length-in-centimeters figure alone. These comparisons are based on typical published average fetal growth curves; actual size varies from pregnancy to pregnancy and is properly assessed via ultrasound, not a calendar estimate.

trimesters.title: The Three Trimesters
trimesters.intro: Each trimester spans a distinct phase of fetal development.

items.title: First Trimester (Weeks 1-12)
items.description: All major organs and body systems begin forming during this period, making it the most developmentally critical window of the entire pregnancy. Many of the more commonly known early pregnancy symptoms (nausea, fatigue, breast tenderness) are most pronounced here, and the risk of miscarriage, while present throughout pregnancy, is statistically highest in this trimester.

items.title: Second Trimester (Weeks 13-26)
items.description: Often called the most comfortable trimester for many people, as early symptoms typically ease while the physical size and discomfort of late pregnancy haven't yet set in. Fetal movement usually becomes noticeable during this period, and a detailed anatomy ultrasound is typically performed around the midpoint to check organ development.

items.title: Third Trimester (Weeks 27-40)
items.description: The fetus gains the majority of its birth weight during this final stretch, while physical discomfort for the pregnant person (back pain, reduced mobility, frequent urination) tends to increase. Prenatal visits typically become more frequent, and this is when full-term status and labor readiness become the primary clinical focus.

items.question: Why is gestational age counted from the last period, not conception?
items.answer: The last menstrual period date is almost always known with confidence, while the exact date of conception is rarely known precisely, since it can occur anywhere within the several-day fertile window around ovulation. Counting from a reliably known date, even though it precedes actual conception by about two weeks, gives a consistent, comparable measure across pregnancies and matches how prenatal care providers date and discuss a pregnancy.

items.question: How accurate are the weekly size comparisons?
items.answer: They're illustrative averages drawn from typical published fetal growth curves, meant to make development easier to visualize — not a personalized or diagnostic measurement. Actual fetal size varies meaningfully between pregnancies and is only properly assessed through ultrasound measurements taken during prenatal care.

items.question: What's the difference between this tracker and a due date calculator?
items.answer: A due date calculator typically answers one specific question — when is the baby likely to arrive — often supporting multiple starting methods (last period, conception date, IVF transfer). This week-by-week tracker instead focuses on the ongoing journey: where the pregnancy currently stands, moving through weeks and trimesters with a size-comparison milestone at each stage.

items.question: Does this tracker account for irregular cycles?
items.answer: No — like the standard 280-day rule it's built on, this tracker assumes a typical 28-day cycle. For irregular cycles, an early ultrasound-based estimate from a healthcare provider is generally considered more accurate than a calculation based on the last period date alone.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: Dividing pregnancy into trimesters and measuring it in gestational weeks from the last menstrual period both stem from Naegele's rule, described by German obstetrician Franz Karl Naegele in his 1830 obstetrics textbook, which established the 280-day (40-week) full-term convention still used today. The "size comparison" style of week-by-week tracking is a much more recent, informal tradition that grew alongside consumer pregnancy books and websites from the late 20th century onward, popularizing fetal development for expectant parents beyond clinical measurements alone.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Modern prenatal care combines LMP-based gestational dating with early ultrasound measurements (typically crown-rump length in the first trimester), which research has shown provides a more accurate estimate of gestational age than LMP alone, particularly for people with irregular cycles or uncertain LMP dates. Digital pregnancy tracking apps and websites, building on the same size-comparison tradition featured here, have become one of the most widely used ways expectant parents follow fetal development week to week, alongside formal prenatal visits.

quickReference.title: The Formulas
quickReference.intro: Every macro is a percentage of total calories, converted to grams by its calorie density.

intro.title: Understanding Macronutrient Splits
intro.paragraph1: "Macros" is short for macronutrients — the three categories of nutrients that supply the body with calories: protein, carbohydrate, and fat (alcohol is sometimes counted as a fourth, but it isn't part of a typical dietary plan). Each gram of protein and carbohydrate supplies about 4 kilocalories, while each gram of fat supplies about 9 — figures known as the Atwater general factors, established in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and still the basis of nutrition labeling today.
intro.paragraph2: This calculator distributes your total daily calories across the three macronutrients as percentages chosen from within the Dietary Reference Intakes' Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (AMDR) — the range of intake for each macronutrient associated with reduced risk of chronic disease while still providing adequate essential nutrients, as established by the U.S. National Academies of Sciences (protein 10-35%, carbohydrate 45-65%, fat 20-35% of total calories). The exact split shifts within that range depending on your selected goal, favoring more protein for fat loss or muscle building and more carbohydrate for a general weight-gain surplus.

goals.title: How Each Goal Changes the Split
goals.intro: The same total calorie number can be divided differently depending on what you're training or eating for.

items.title: Lose Weight — 30% Protein / 45% Carbs / 25% Fat
items.description: During a calorie deficit, higher relative protein intake is associated with better preservation of lean muscle mass, which is why this split leans toward the upper end of the AMDR protein range compared to a maintenance split.

items.title: Maintain Weight — 20% Protein / 50% Carbs / 30% Fat
items.description: A balanced distribution suited to sustaining current body weight and typical daily activity, comfortably within the middle of the AMDR for all three macronutrients.

items.title: Gain Weight — 20% Protein / 55% Carbs / 25% Fat
items.description: A general calorie surplus for weight gain leans on additional carbohydrate to fuel the surplus, since protein needs don't necessarily scale up as much as total calorie needs do for non-training-focused weight gain.

items.title: Build Muscle — 30% Protein / 50% Carbs / 20% Fat
items.description: Supporting muscle protein synthesis alongside resistance training benefits from higher protein intake, consistent with sports-nutrition research on protein needs during a training-driven surplus (often expressed elsewhere as 1.6-2.2 g per kg of body weight).

examples.title: Worked Examples

items.question: Where do these calorie totals come from?
items.answer: You provide your total daily calorie target directly, or optionally import it from this site's TDEE Calculator (which estimates it from your BMR, activity level, and weight goal). This tool focuses purely on how to split a calorie total you already know into macronutrients — it doesn't estimate your calorie needs itself.

items.question: Why do the percentages differ by goal instead of using one fixed split?
items.answer: Protein needs in particular respond to context: research on body composition consistently shows that higher relative protein intake helps preserve muscle during a calorie deficit and supports muscle growth during a training-driven surplus, while a simple maintenance diet doesn't need to push toward either extreme. All four splits still stay within the nationally recognized AMDR, so none of them is an extreme or fad-diet ratio.

items.question: What if I know my ideal protein intake in grams per kilogram instead of a percentage?
items.answer: You can still use this tool as a starting point and then manually adjust: multiply your body weight in kilograms by your target g/kg protein figure to get grams of protein directly, convert that to calories (× 4), and treat the remaining calories as the total to split between carbohydrate and fat using whichever ratio suits your preference.

items.question: Are these macronutrient splits appropriate for everyone?
items.answer: They're general, population-level estimates within accepted scientific ranges, not personalized medical or athletic nutrition advice. People with specific medical conditions (kidney disease, diabetes), pregnant or breastfeeding people, and competitive athletes with specialized needs should work with a registered dietitian or physician to set macronutrient targets appropriate to their specific situation.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The idea of counting food in terms of its energy-yielding components traces back to 19th-century chemist Wilbur Olin Atwater, whose extensive combustion and metabolism experiments at Wesleyan University established the "Atwater general factors" (4 kcal/g for protein and carbohydrate, 9 kcal/g for fat) still printed on nutrition labels worldwide today. "Macro counting" as a popular dieting framework — deliberately hitting daily gram targets for each macronutrient rather than just a single calorie number — became widespread within bodybuilding and fitness communities starting in the 1990s and 2000s, building directly on Atwater's century-old energy conversion factors.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The scientific consensus on macronutrient ranges was formalized by the U.S. National Academies of Sciences (then the Institute of Medicine) in its 2005 Dietary Reference Intakes report, which established the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Ranges this calculator's splits are built from. More recent sports-nutrition research, particularly position stands from the International Society of Sports Nutrition, has further refined protein recommendations specifically for people engaged in resistance training or caloric restriction, generally supporting a higher relative protein intake than the population-wide average — the basis for this calculator's goal-specific adjustments within the broader accepted range.

bmr-calculator.disclaimer: This tool provides a general, educational estimate only and is not a substitute for personalized advice from a registered dietitian, physician, or other qualified healthcare provider — actual metabolic rate can only be measured precisely with clinical indirect calorimetry.

quickReference.title: The Formulas
quickReference.intro: Both equations estimate BMR from the same three measurements — weight, height, and age — combined differently.

intro.title: Understanding Basal Metabolic Rate
intro.paragraph1: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) is the number of calories your body burns at complete rest to sustain basic life-supporting functions — breathing, circulation, cell production, and maintaining body temperature — with no digestion, movement, or other activity factored in. It typically accounts for 60-75% of total daily calorie burn for most people, making it the largest single component of daily energy expenditure, even though it doesn't include the calories burned through physical activity or digesting food (Total Daily Energy Expenditure, or TDEE, adds those factors on top of BMR).
intro.paragraph2: Because BMR can only be measured precisely in a lab setting using indirect calorimetry (measuring oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production while at complete rest), predictive equations based on easily measured variables — weight, height, age, and sex — were developed to estimate it without specialized equipment. This calculator implements the two most historically significant of these equations side by side, letting you see both a formula from over a century ago and the one that superseded it in clinical preference.

formulas.title: The Two Formulas
formulas.intro: Both equations use the same four inputs but combine them with different coefficients, reflecting different source populations and eras of measurement.

items.title: Harris-Benedict (1919)
items.description: Developed by James Arthur Harris and Francis Gano Benedict from data on a few hundred subjects, this was the first widely adopted equation for estimating resting metabolism and remained the clinical standard for over 60 years. A 1984 revision by Roza and Shizgal adjusted its coefficients slightly, but the version shown here is the original 1919 form for direct historical comparison.

items.title: Mifflin-St Jeor (1990)
items.description: Developed by Mark Mifflin and Sachiko St Jeor using a larger and more contemporary subject group with more accurate body composition measurement than was available in 1919, this equation has been repeatedly validated as more accurate for the modern general adult population and is the formula the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics currently recommends as the default choice.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A couple of measurement sets and what each formula returns.

items.question: Which formula should I trust more?
items.answer: The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics recommends Mifflin-St Jeor as the more accurate equation for most of today's general adult population, since it was developed from more recent and more representative data. Harris-Benedict remains useful as the historical reference point and is still cited in some clinical and research contexts, but Mifflin-St Jeor is the better default choice for most people today.

items.question: Why do the two formulas give different numbers for the same person?
items.answer: They were built from different subject populations measured six decades apart, using different statistical methods available at the time. Body composition norms, measurement precision, and the demographic makeup of the study samples all differ between 1919 and 1990, which is reflected in each formula's specific coefficients — the gap between them for any individual is typically modest but not zero.

items.question: Why doesn't this calculator include activity level or a calorie target?
items.answer: This tool deliberately focuses on the single BMR number and the historical/scientific comparison between the two equations that estimate it, without adding the extra variables (activity multiplier, weight goal) that a Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE) calculator layers on top of BMR. If you want a full daily calorie target, this site's separate TDEE Calculator builds on BMR with exactly those additional factors.

items.question: Are these formulas accurate for everyone?
items.answer: Both are population-average equations validated primarily on people of typical body composition; they tend to be less accurate for people who are very muscular, very lean, or have obesity, since neither formula directly measures body fat or muscle mass. For those cases, a formula that incorporates body fat percentage (like Katch-McArdle) or a direct clinical measurement is generally more accurate.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The Harris-Benedict equation was published in 1919 by American scientists James Arthur Harris and Francis Gano Benedict at the Carnegie Institution's Nutrition Laboratory, based on metabolic measurements of a few hundred men and women — a landmark early attempt to predict resting metabolism from simple body measurements rather than requiring direct measurement for every individual. It became the standard reference formula in clinical nutrition and medicine for the following six decades, undergoing a minor coefficient revision by Roza and Shizgal in 1984.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: In 1990, Mark D. Mifflin and Sachiko T. St Jeor published a new equation derived from a larger, more demographically diverse, and more recently measured subject pool, using body composition assessment methods more advanced than those available to Harris and Benedict seven decades earlier. Multiple subsequent validation studies comparing predictive equations against measured resting metabolic rate (via indirect calorimetry) have found Mifflin-St Jeor more accurate for the general adult population on average, leading the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics to recommend it as the preferred equation in the absence of direct measurement.

date-calculator.title: Date Calculator
date-calculator.description: Find the difference between two dates in days, weeks, months, and years, or add/subtract a duration from a date.

quickReference.title: The Math
quickReference.intro: Every calculation here is either a calendar subtraction or a calendar addition.

intro.title: Understanding Date Arithmetic
intro.paragraph1: Calculating with calendar dates is more involved than simple arithmetic because months have unequal lengths (28 to 31 days), years can be leap years (366 days instead of 365), and "a month later" doesn't mean a fixed number of days — adding one month to January 31st, for instance, can't literally produce February 31st, since February never has that many days. This calculator handles those irregularities automatically so you get a real, valid calendar date or an accurate day count every time.
intro.paragraph2: The two most common date questions — "how far apart are these two dates?" and "what date is a certain duration from now?" — both come up constantly in everyday planning: tracking an anniversary or a deadline, calculating someone's exact age, figuring out a project's end date from its start and duration, or working out when a warranty or subscription period will lapse.

modes.title: The Two Modes
modes.intro: Each mode answers one of the two most common calendar questions.

items.title: Date Difference
items.description: Given two dates, this mode reports the total number of days and weeks between them, plus a broken-down years/months/days figure (the way a person would naturally describe an age or a length of time, rather than one large day count).

items.title: Add/Subtract
items.description: Given a starting date and a duration in days, weeks, months, or years, this mode calculates the resulting date — handling month-length and leap-year edge cases automatically, including clamping an out-of-range day (like January 31st plus one month) to the last valid day of the target month.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few common date questions, computed the same way this tool computes them.

items.question: Why does adding a month to January 31st give February 28th instead of March 3rd?
items.answer: This calculator uses "clamping" behavior: adding a month keeps the day number the same when possible, and if the target month doesn't have that many days, it lands on the target month's actual last day rather than overflowing into the next month. This matches how most people intuitively mean "one month later" and is the same convention used by most calendar software.

items.question: How are leap years handled?
items.answer: This calculator determines leap years using the standard Gregorian calendar rule (a year is a leap year if divisible by 4, except century years, which must be divisible by 400), so February 29th is correctly included in day counts and date arithmetic only in years where it actually exists.

items.question: Why is the years/months/days breakdown different from just dividing total days?
items.answer: A calendar-aware breakdown accounts for the actual varying lengths of the months and years spanned, which is why it can't be produced by simply dividing the total day count by 30 or 365 — doing that would give an approximate but often noticeably inaccurate answer, especially over date ranges spanning leap years or months of different lengths.

items.question: Does it matter which date I put first in Date Difference mode?
items.answer: No — this tool always reports the absolute span between the two dates regardless of which one you enter as the start or end, though it will note if the date you labeled "end" actually comes chronologically before the one you labeled "start."

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The calendar this calculator uses — the Gregorian calendar — was introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582 as a refinement of the earlier Julian calendar, correcting a small but compounding drift between the calendar year and the actual solar year. Its defining leap-year rule (skipping the leap day in century years not divisible by 400) was specifically designed to keep the calendar aligned with the seasons over long timescales, and it remains the internationally accepted civil calendar used by nearly every country today.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Modern computing systems represent dates and times using standards like ISO 8601 (the YYYY-MM-DD date format) and Unix time (a count of seconds since January 1, 1970), which make date arithmetic across time zones, calendars, and software systems consistent and unambiguous. Programming libraries built on these standards — like the one powering this calculator — handle the many calendar edge cases (leap years, varying month lengths, daylight saving transitions) so that applications don't need to reimplement calendar logic from scratch.

quickReference.title: The Math
quickReference.intro: Every duration is converted to total seconds, combined, and converted back.

intro.title: Understanding Duration Arithmetic
intro.paragraph1: Adding or subtracting durations expressed in hours, minutes, and seconds requires carrying values between units, much like adding numbers in a non-decimal base: 60 seconds carry into 1 minute, and 60 minutes carry into 1 hour, rather than the base-10 carrying used in ordinary arithmetic. This calculator converts both durations to a single total-seconds value, performs the addition or subtraction on that single number, then converts the result back into hours, minutes, and seconds for display.
intro.paragraph2: It's worth distinguishing duration arithmetic (the kind this tool performs) from clock-time arithmetic. Duration arithmetic answers "how long is 1 hour 45 minutes plus 30 minutes?" as a pure elapsed-time question, while clock-time arithmetic answers "what time will it be 3 hours after 11:00 PM?", which wraps around a 24-hour cycle and depends on a specific starting point on the clock. This tool handles the former; subtracting a larger duration from a smaller one correctly produces a negative result rather than wrapping around.

useCases.title: Common Uses
useCases.intro: Duration arithmetic comes up whenever total elapsed time needs to be tracked or combined.

items.title: Tracking Work or Study Time
items.description: Adding up several timed sessions (like a stopwatch-tracked work sprint or study block) to find a total elapsed duration for the day or week.

items.title: Cooking and Recipe Timing
items.description: Combining multiple sequential cooking steps (prep time plus cook time plus resting time) into a single total duration for planning when a dish needs to go in the oven.

items.title: Video and Audio Editing
items.description: Adding up clip lengths to find a total runtime, or finding the difference between two timestamps to determine a clip's exact duration.

examples.intro: A few duration calculations, computed the same way this tool computes them.

items.question: Why is the result sometimes negative?
items.answer: When subtracting, if the second duration is longer than the first, the result represents a deficit rather than a remaining amount — the calculator reports this as a negative duration rather than silently reporting an incorrect positive number or wrapping around a clock.

items.question: Is this the same as adding two clock times, like 3:00 PM plus 2:15?
items.answer: Not quite — this tool adds and subtracts elapsed durations (like "1 hour 30 minutes of work"), not points on a 24-hour clock. Adding a duration to a specific clock time to find a new clock time is a related but distinct calculation, since it involves wrapping around midnight and knowing AM/PM, which this tool doesn't handle.

items.question: What's the maximum number of hours I can enter?
items.answer: There's no fixed upper limit built into the duration format — you can enter any number of hours (for example, 100 hours for a multi-day total), since hours aren't constrained to the 0-23 range the way minutes and seconds are constrained to 0-59.

items.question: Why do minutes and seconds have to be less than 60?
items.answer: A time value like "1 hour, 75 minutes" is not in its simplest, standard form — 75 minutes should be expressed as 1 hour 15 minutes. Requiring minutes and seconds to stay under 60 keeps each input in the normalized format that duration arithmetic expects, avoiding ambiguity about how a non-standard value should be interpreted.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: The base-60 (sexagesimal) system used for dividing hours into minutes and minutes into seconds originates from ancient Babylonian mathematics, dating back over 4,000 years. Babylonian scribes favored base 60 in part because 60 has many divisors (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30), making fractions like a third or a quarter of an hour land on whole numbers of minutes — a practical convenience that a base-10 system for time would lack.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: While the sexagesimal hour/minute/second structure has remained essentially unchanged since antiquity, modern computing represents durations internally using standardized formats — commonly a single count of seconds or milliseconds — precisely so that duration arithmetic (the kind this calculator performs) can be done with simple numeric operations before being converted back into the human-readable hours/minutes/seconds format for display, exactly as this tool does internally.

dice-roller.title: Dice Roller
dice-roller.description: Roll customizable virtual dice (d4, d6, d8, d10, d12, d20) and keep a history of your rolls.

result.heading: Result
result.invalidDiceCount: Enter a number of dice between 1 and 20.
result.invalidFaces: Choose one of the supported die types.

quickReference.title: The Math
quickReference.intro: Each die independently produces a uniformly random whole number from 1 to its number of faces.

intro.title: Understanding Dice Probability
intro.paragraph1: A fair die with n faces produces each of its possible outcomes (1 through n) with equal probability, 1/n, on every roll, independent of any previous roll — a property called being "memoryless." This tool simulates that behavior using a pseudorandom number generator: each roll draws a random value uniformly between 1 and the selected number of faces, so over many rolls the outcomes converge toward the same 1/n frequency a fair physical die would produce.
intro.paragraph2: Rolling multiple dice at once changes the shape of the total's distribution even though each individual die stays uniform. A single d6 roll is equally likely to land on any face from 1 to 6, but the sum of two d6 dice is not uniform — totals near 7 (the middle of the possible range of 2 to 12) are far more common than totals near 2 or 12, because there are more combinations of two dice that add up to 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1) than combinations that add up to 2 (only 1+1) or 12 (only 6+6). This is the same principle behind the bell-shaped distribution seen in board games and tabletop role-playing dice pools.

useCases.intro: Virtual dice rolling shows up anywhere a fair, unpredictable outcome is needed.

items.title: Tabletop and Role-Playing Games

items.title: Board Games and Party Games

items.title: Teaching Probability and Statistics
items.description: Demonstrating concepts like uniform distributions, expected value, and the law of large numbers by rolling (simulated) dice many times and observing the results converge toward theoretical probabilities.

items.question: Are these rolls truly random?
items.answer: This tool uses your browser's built-in pseudorandom number generator, which is statistically uniform and unpredictable enough for games, teaching, and casual use, though it is not a cryptographically secure source of randomness suitable for security-sensitive applications.

items.question: Why does the total of multiple dice cluster around the middle?
items.answer: Because there are more ways to combine dice to reach a middle total than an extreme one. With two d6, only one combination (1+1) produces a total of 2, but six combinations produce a total of 7, making 7 six times more likely than 2.

items.question: What's the maximum number of dice I can roll at once?
items.answer: This tool supports rolling up to 20 dice at a time, which comfortably covers dice pools used in tabletop games and most classroom probability demonstrations.

items.question: Why are d4, d6, d8, d10, d12, and d20 the standard die types?
items.answer: These correspond to the five Platonic solids (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron) plus the ten-sided die, all of which have faces of equal size and shape, ensuring every outcome is equally likely when the die is fair and evenly weighted.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: Dice are among the oldest gaming objects known to archaeology, with cube-shaped dice found at sites in the Middle East and the Indus Valley dating back roughly 5,000 years, and even earlier astragali (animal knucklebones used as proto-dice) found at Neolithic sites. The now-standard set of polyhedral dice (d4 through d20) used in modern tabletop role-playing games was popularized in the 1970s alongside the rise of games like Dungeons & Dragons, though dice shaped as the Platonic solids date back to ancient Greece and Rome.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Digital dice rollers like this one rely on pseudorandom number generation algorithms, which use deterministic mathematical formulas seeded by unpredictable inputs (like system time or hardware entropy) to produce sequences of numbers that pass statistical tests for randomness. This makes physical dice unnecessary for the vast majority of casual gaming and educational contexts, while true random number generators, based on physical processes like atmospheric noise or radioactive decay, remain reserved for higher-stakes applications like cryptography.

intro.title: Understanding This Tool
intro.paragraph1: This calculator takes the two names you enter, combines and normalizes them, and runs them through a deterministic numerical formula that converts the letters into a percentage between 0 and 100. Because the formula is deterministic, the same two names will always produce the same percentage no matter how many times you check, and the order you enter them in doesn't matter either — "Alex and Jordan" gives the same result as "Jordan and Alex."
intro.disclaimer: Important: this percentage is generated purely for entertainment. It has no basis in psychology, relationship science, or any real measure of compatibility — it is simply a playful numbers game based on the letters in a name.

useCases.title: Common Uses
useCases.intro: Name-based love calculators are a long-running piece of internet and schoolyard culture, used for lighthearted fun rather than serious decision-making.

items.title: Icebreakers and Party Games
items.description: A quick, playful activity among friends or at parties, similar to fortune-telling games like magic 8-balls or paper fortune tellers.

items.title: Social Media and Sharing
items.description: Generating a shareable, lighthearted percentage to post or send to friends purely for laughs.

items.title: Nostalgic Fun
items.description: Recreating the classic schoolyard notebook game of testing name compatibility, now as a quick digital version.

items.question: Is this a real measure of compatibility?
items.answer: No. This tool is designed purely for entertainment. Real relationship compatibility depends on factors like shared values, communication, trust, and effort — none of which can be measured from the spelling of a name.

items.question: Why do I get the same percentage every time for the same two names?
items.answer: The calculator uses a deterministic formula: it always transforms the same input letters into the same output number. This is intentional, so the "result" for a specific pair of names stays consistent, similar to how a fortune-telling game gives a memorable, repeatable answer.

items.question: Does the order I type the names in matter?
items.answer: No — the tool treats "Alex and Jordan" the same as "Jordan and Alex" by sorting the two names before combining them, so the percentage is always symmetric regardless of input order.

items.question: Can I use names in any language or alphabet?
items.answer: Yes. The formula works on the underlying characters of whatever name you type, whether it uses Latin, Arabic, Devanagari, or any other script, so it works the same way across all supported languages on this site.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: Name-based compatibility games have a long history in popular culture, from the pen-and-paper "FLAMES" game played by schoolchildren (an acronym for Friends, Lovers, Affectionate, Marriage, Enemies, Siblings) to numerology traditions that assign numeric values to letters and interpret the results. These games spread from playgrounds and magazines to the early internet in the 1990s and 2000s, becoming one of the first widely popular categories of novelty calculator websites.

realCompatibility.title: What Actually Predicts Compatibility
realCompatibility.paragraph: Decades of relationship research point to very different factors than a name's letters. Psychologist John Gottman's long-term studies of couples identified patterns like the ratio of positive to negative interactions, how partners handle conflict, and mutual respect and admiration as strong predictors of relationship success — see the reference below for a starting point into that body of research. If you're curious about real compatibility, communication skills, shared values, and how a couple handles disagreements tend to matter far more than any calculator ever could.

fuel-cost-calculator.description: Estimate the fuel cost of a trip from distance, fuel consumption rate, and fuel price.

form.rateValueHintConsumption: How much fuel your vehicle uses per 100 distance units (e.g. 8 L per 100 km).
form.rateValueHintEfficiency: How far your vehicle travels per unit of fuel (e.g. 12.5 km per liter, or 30 miles per gallon).

quickReference.title: The Math
quickReference.intro: The calculation depends on which rate type you choose, but both end with cost = fuel used × price.

intro.title: Understanding Fuel Cost Estimation
intro.paragraph1: Estimating the fuel cost of a trip comes down to figuring out how much fuel the trip will consume, then multiplying that amount by the price of fuel. Fuel usage itself can be described in two mathematically equivalent but differently worded ways: as a consumption rate (how much fuel is used per fixed distance, like liters per 100 kilometers, common in most of the world) or as an efficiency rate (how far a vehicle travels per unit of fuel, like kilometers per liter or miles per gallon, common in the United States and United Kingdom).
intro.paragraph2: The two rate types are just inverses of each other rearranged for convenience: a car using 8 liters per 100 km is exactly as efficient as one traveling 12.5 km per liter (since 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5). This calculator accepts either style directly, so you don't need to convert your vehicle's fuel economy figures into a different format before estimating a trip's cost — you just need to keep the distance unit and the fuel-rate's distance unit consistent (both in kilometers, or both in miles).

useCases.title: Common Uses
useCases.intro: Fuel cost estimation is useful anywhere a trip's cost needs to be planned or compared in advance.

items.title: Road Trip Budgeting
items.description: Estimating the total fuel cost for a long drive before setting out, to plan a travel budget alongside accommodation and food costs.

items.title: Comparing Vehicles
items.description: Comparing the running cost of two different vehicles with different fuel efficiency ratings over the same regular commute or route.

items.title: Ride-Sharing and Delivery Cost Splitting
items.description: Estimating a fair per-person or per-delivery fuel cost contribution based on the distance driven and the vehicle's fuel efficiency.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: A few fuel cost calculations, computed the same way this tool computes them.

items.question: Which rate type should I use?
items.answer: Use whichever figure your vehicle's manual or dashboard already shows. Most of the world (Europe, most of Asia) reports fuel consumption in liters per 100 km, while the United States and United Kingdom typically report fuel efficiency in miles per gallon.

items.question: Do I need to convert kilometers to miles or liters to gallons?
items.answer: No — this calculator does not perform unit conversions between measurement systems. Just make sure the distance you enter and the distance unit implied by your rate figure match (both kilometers, or both miles), and that your price is per the same fuel unit (liter or gallon) as your rate figure.

items.question: Does this account for traffic, terrain, or driving style?
items.answer: No. This calculator uses a single, fixed fuel-consumption rate that you provide, and assumes it applies uniformly across the whole trip. Real-world fuel economy varies with traffic, road grade, speed, cargo weight, and driving habits, so treat the result as an estimate rather than an exact prediction.

items.question: What does "cost per distance unit" mean?
items.answer: It's the total trip cost divided by the total distance, giving you a per-kilometer or per-mile cost figure that's useful for comparing trips of different lengths or comparing against a per-mile reimbursement rate.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: Fuel economy measurement became a matter of public and regulatory interest following the 1973 oil crisis, when fuel shortages and price spikes pushed governments to require standardized fuel economy labeling on new vehicles. The United States introduced Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards in 1975, reported in miles per gallon, while most of the rest of the world adopted the liters-per-100-kilometers convention, which has the practical advantage that a lower number always means better efficiency (unlike miles per gallon, where a higher number is better, making direct differences less intuitive to compare).

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Modern vehicles include onboard trip computers that estimate real-time and average fuel consumption using data from the engine control unit, though official fuel economy ratings (like those from the EPA in the United States or the WLTP test procedure in the European Union) are measured under standardized laboratory conditions that may not exactly match real-world driving, which is why real-world fuel costs often run somewhat higher than the official rating would suggest.

batch-invoice-calculator.description: Build multiple invoices with line items and tax, and track a running total across all of them. Saved in your browser.

quickReference.title: The Math
quickReference.intro: Every invoice is calculated the same way, then all saved invoices are added together for the running summary.

intro.title: Understanding Batch Invoicing
intro.paragraph1: This tool separates two related but distinct calculations: computing a single invoice's total (line items summed into a subtotal, with tax applied on top), and aggregating many already-computed invoices into a running summary. Each invoice can carry its own tax rate, since real businesses sometimes bill different clients, product categories, or jurisdictions at different tax rates within the same batch of work.
intro.paragraph2: Everything you save is stored only in your own browser (using its local storage), not on a server — which means your invoice data stays private to your device, but also means it won't appear on a different browser or device, and clearing your browser's site data will remove it. This makes the tool well suited for quick batch calculations — like totaling a stack of paper receipts, or reconciling a month's worth of client invoices — without creating accounts or uploading financial data anywhere.

useCases.title: Common Uses
useCases.intro: Aggregating multiple invoices into one running total comes up in everyday small-business and freelance bookkeeping.

items.title: Freelance and Contractor Billing
items.description: Tracking several client invoices issued over a week or month and seeing the combined total, tax owed, and invoice count at a glance.

items.title: Small Business Expense Reconciliation
items.description: Re-entering a stack of paper or PDF invoices from suppliers to get an accurate combined total for a bookkeeping period, without opening spreadsheet software.

items.title: Quarterly or Monthly Tax Preparation
items.description: Quickly separating the tax portion from the pre-tax amount across many invoices, to get the two totals a tax filing typically requires.

items.question: Where is my invoice data stored?
items.answer: Entirely in your own browser's local storage, on your own device. It is never uploaded to a server, which means it stays private, but it also means it won't sync across different browsers or devices, and it will be lost if you clear your browser's site data.

items.question: Can I edit an invoice after saving it?
items.answer: Yes — click the edit (pencil) icon next to any saved invoice in the table to load it back into the form above, make your changes, and click "Update This Invoice" to save the changes in place.

items.question: Does each invoice need its own tax rate?
items.answer: Yes, the tax rate is set per invoice rather than globally, since a batch of invoices might mix different tax rates — for example, some tax-exempt items alongside standard-rate items, or clients in different tax jurisdictions.

items.question: Is this the same as the Invoice Generator tool?
items.answer: No — the Invoice Generator creates one polished, printable invoice document with your business details and a client's details. This tool is built for the opposite direction: totaling up many already-created invoices to answer "how much have I billed in total this month, and how much of that is tax?"

items.question: What does the Print/Export button do?
items.answer: It opens your browser's print dialog with a clean, formatted view of your saved invoice list and running summary — from there you can print a physical copy or choose "Save as PDF" (available in most browsers' print dialogs) to export it as a file.

history.title: History and Origin
history.paragraph: Invoices are among the oldest documented business records, with clay tablets recording itemized goods, quantities, and totals found in ancient Mesopotamia dating back over 5,000 years — some of the earliest known writing was, in fact, accounting records. The systematic bookkeeping methods behind modern invoicing and batch reconciliation trace back to Luca Pacioli's 1494 treatise Summa de Arithmetica, which described the double-entry bookkeeping system used by Venetian merchants and is widely credited as the foundation of modern accounting. The core structure of an invoice (itemized quantities and prices summed into a total, sometimes with a tax or duty added) has remained conceptually unchanged for centuries, even as the medium moved from paper ledgers to digital spreadsheets and invoicing software.

dataPrivacy.title: Local-Only Data Storage
dataPrivacy.paragraph: This tool uses your browser's built-in local storage feature to remember your saved invoices between visits, rather than sending any data to a remote server. This is a deliberate privacy-first design choice for a tool handling financial figures: your invoice numbers, vendor names, and amounts never leave your device. The tradeoff is that this data is tied to one specific browser on one specific device — it won't be available if you switch browsers, use a different computer, or clear your browsing data.

faq.question: Is embedding free?
faq.answer: Yes — embedding any TooloraLabs tool is completely free, with no signup, API key, or usage limit.

faq.question: Does the embedded calculator update automatically?
faq.answer: Yes. The iframe loads the live tool directly from TooloraLabs, so any future improvements to the calculator appear automatically on your site without you needing to change anything.

faq.question: Can I remove the "Powered by TooloraLabs" link?
faq.answer: No — the credit link is a condition of free embedding. It's small, unobtrusive, and opens in a new tab so it doesn't take visitors away from your page.

faq.question: Will the embedded tool match my site's design?
faq.answer: The embed uses TooloraLabs' own light-background styling inside its iframe boundary, which keeps it visually self-contained and consistent regardless of your site's own theme.

faq.question: Which tools can I embed?
faq.answer: We're rolling out embeddable versions tool by tool, starting with the BMI Calculator. More tools will be added to the list above over time.

guidance.title: Buying a house?
guidance.body: Use the Mortgage Calculator. It's the only one of the three built around property-specific details like a down payment, property tax, homeowners insurance, and private mortgage insurance (PMI) — none of which apply to a general installment loan.

guidance.title: Financing a car, education, or anything else?
guidance.body: Use the Loan Calculator. It's a simpler, general-purpose amortization calculator for any fixed-rate installment loan, without the property-specific fields a mortgage needs.

guidance.title: Saving or investing money instead of borrowing it?
guidance.body: Use the Compound Interest Calculator. It's the only one of the three that models money growing over time rather than money being paid off — the mortgage and loan calculators both assume you're the one making payments, not the one receiving interest.
